Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 65, verse 1 (part 1 of 3):

﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at their waiting period (ʿiddah)﴾.

Addressing the Prophet (ﷺ) with the address is a style of the verses of legislation that are concerned with a matter, and this does not necessitate restricting what is mentioned after it to the Prophet (ﷺ), like ﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight﴾ [al-Anfal: 65], because the Prophet (ﷺ) is the one who undertakes the implementation of the Sharia among his community and the clarification of its affairs. If the legislation that comes includes him and includes the community, the address comes including what indicates that, like the plural form in His saying here, ﴿when you divorce women﴾. And if the legislation is specific to the Messenger (ﷺ), it comes with what necessitates that, like ﴿O Messenger, deliver what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67].

Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: "This is the saying of those who hold that the address is to him in wording, while the meaning is to him and to the believers. When Allah intends the address to the believers, He softens it with His saying ﴿O Prophet﴾, and when the address is entirely to him in both wording and meaning, He says ﴿O Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41]." End of quote. The reason for the concern with the rulings of divorce, reconciliation and the waiting period, we will mention at His saying, ﴿and fear Allah, your Lord﴾.

The rulings mentioned in this surah are general for the Muslims. So the plural pronoun in His saying ﴿when you divorce women﴾ and what follows of pronouns are like it, meant to include him and his community. The address is directed to him because he is the one who conveys to people, the leader of his community, their exemplar, and the one who implements Allah's rulings among them in their dealings with one another. So the implied meaning is: "when you divorce, O Muslims."

The apparent meaning of the word (idha, "when") is the future, and this supports what Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said, that it is

the beginning of a legislation. They said it is permissible that what is meant is: when you divorce in the future, then do not return to the like of what you did, but divorce them at their waiting period, i.e., at their periods of purity, as will come.

The repetition of the verb (﴿fa-tallequhunna﴾, "then divorce them") is for the greater emphasis on it. He did not say "when you divorce women, then at their purity." A parallel to this has preceded at His saying, ﴿and when you seize, you seize as tyrants﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 130] in Surat al-Shu'ara, and His saying ﴿and when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72] in Surat al-Furqan.

The lam in (﴿li-iddatihinna﴾, "at their waiting period") is the lam of time, and it has the meaning of "at," like "it was written for such a day of such a month." From it is His saying ﴿establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra: 78]. This lam does not admit any other of the meanings that the lam comes with. Since the object of the lam here is not a time, it is known that what is meant is the time attached to their waiting period, i.e., the time of purity.

The meaning of the construction is that the waiting period of the women has been made a time for pronouncing their divorce, so the waiting period is used as a metonymy for the purity, because the divorced woman observes her waiting period through periods of purity.

The benefit of this is that it be an allusion to the wisdom of this legislation, which is that divorce should occur at the beginning of the waiting period. The waiting period begins with the first purity of three purities, in order to ward off harm from the divorced woman by prolonging the wait for her remarriage. For the days between her menstruation when she is divorced and her purity are not counted in her waiting period. So most divorcers intended by this to prolong the period of the waiting period, so that they might give themselves room for deliberation about reconciliation before she separates from them.

The verb (﴿tallaqtum﴾, "you divorce") is used in the sense of "you intend to divorce," and this is a established usage. From it is His saying ﴿O you who believe, when you rise to the prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and the context is clear.

The verse indicates the permissibility of divorce by implication, because the Qur'an does not presuppose the occurrence of a forbidden act without clarifying its prohibition.

Divorce is permissible because it may be a necessity for some spouses, for the two persons are, in most cases, joined by a recent relationship in which there was previously no tie of lineage, neighborhood, or a similar or comparable disposition. So it often happens after marriage that a disagreement arises between them in some aspects of living together, which may be severe and difficult to resolve, so one of them becomes weary, and there is no way to relieve them of that except separation between them. So Allah permitted it because it is a necessity, but He permitted it only to remove harm. Therefore the permission for it should not be made a means for one spouse to harm the other, or for a relative of either, or for the purpose of changing tastes. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The most hateful of lawful things to Allah is divorce."

The linking of (﴿tallaqtum﴾) to the conditional (idha) suggests that divorce is contrary to the original state in the relationship between spouses, about which Allah said ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you mates from yourselves that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy﴾ [al-Rum: 21].

Scholars differed on whether the Prophet (ﷺ) divorced. Al-Khattabi, in his commentary on the Sunan of Abu Dawud, affirmed it, but the Prophet's divorce is not established by a sound hadith. The narrations on this are two reports. The first is what Ibn Majah related from Suwayd ibn Sa'id, ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmir ibn Zurarah, and Masruq ibn al-Marzuban, with their chain to Ibn ʿAbbas, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divorced Hafsah and then took her back." In this chain there is weakness, because Suwayd ibn Sa'id is weak; Ibn Ma'in attributed lying to him, and Ibn al-Madini, al-Nasa'i and Ibn ʿAdi declared him weak, though Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Abu Hatim accepted him. Masruq ibn al-Marzuban is also declared weak. ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmir ibn Zurarah remains with nothing spoken against him, so the hadith would be sound but strange, and a strange report is not accepted in matters whose transmission is widely demanded, like this. This hadith is strange at its beginning and its end, due to Sa'id ibn Jubayr's sole narration of it from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn ʿAbbas's sole narration of it from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, while the people of the Sahih did not include it. So the more likely view is that the Prophet's divorce of Hafsah did not occur, but the matter concerned an oath of abstinence (iilaʾ) due to Hafsah.

What is known in the Sahih from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab is that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took an oath of abstinence from his wives, and the people said, 'The Messenger of Allah has divorced his wives.' ʿUmar said: I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, did you divorce your wives?' He said: 'No. I took an oath of abstinence from them for a month.'" Perhaps one of the narrators from Ibn ʿAbbas expressed the iilaʾ with the wording of divorce, and the return (fayʾah) with the wording of "returned" to him. Ibn Majah is also weak according to the critics.

The second is the hadith of al-Jawniyyah, named Asma' or Umaymah bint Sharahil al-Kindiyyah, in the Sahih, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married her, and when he entered upon her to consummate, she said to him: 'I seek refuge in Allah from you.' He said: 'You have sought refuge in one who grants refuge. Join your family,' and he commanded Abu Usayd al-Sa'idi to clothe her with two garments and to send her back to her family." Perhaps she intended to show her nobility and to display that she has no desire for men, which is a common trait among women.

The more likely view is that this was a divorce, and that it occurred upon her request. So it is like the choice (takhyir) about which Allah said ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: if you desire the life of this world﴾ [al-Ahzab: 28] in Surat al-Ahzab. Thus this does not contradict his saying "The most hateful of lawful things to Allah is divorce," since that saying applies to divorce that the husband initiates by his own motive, because the reason for the dislike is what divorce leaves behind of resentment in the divorced woman toward the one who divorces her. So the Prophet (ﷺ) would not initiate it, to avoid the divorced woman harboring resentment toward him, which would be a burden upon her. But when she asks him, the means that must be blocked no longer exists.

It is known from His saying (﴿li-iddatihinna﴾) that they are the women who have been consummated with, because those not consummated with have no waiting period, by consensus, according to the text of the verse in al-Ahzab.

This verse is a proof for Malik, al-Shafiʿi and the majority that the waiting period is by the periods of purity, not by menstruation. For the verse indicates that the pronouncement of divorce should occur at the beginning of the waiting period. So if the beginning of the waiting period were menstruation, the verse would be a command to pronounce divorce during menstruation, and there is no disagreement that this is forbidden, due to the hadith of ʿUmar in the case of his son ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar divorcing his wife while she was menstruating. The scholars agreed to act upon it. How then would someone oppose the meaning of "qurʾ" with a disagreement that leads to nullifying the ruling in the case of Ibn ʿUmar? The waiting period had already been legislated earlier by the verse in Surat al-Baqarah and the verses of al-Ahzab, so that tying the pronouncement of divorce to the state in which the waiting period occurs is a referral to a matter known to them.

The wisdom of the waiting period has been explained earlier.

* * *

﴿And count the waiting period﴾.

Ihsa' (counting, reckoning): knowing and precisely fixing the count. It is derived from al-hasa, which are small stones, because when the numbers of something became large, they would assign to each counted item a pebble, then count those pebbles. Allah said ﴿and He has counted all things in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 28].

The meaning: the command to precisely observe the days of the waiting period, completing all of them, and not being lax about them, because laxity about them is a means to one of two matters. Either remarriage before its completion, so that lineage may be confused, or prolonging the period upon the divorced woman during the days of her prohibition from remarriage, since during the waiting period she is not free from need of someone to take care of her. And also the lapse of the time for reconciliation if the divorcer had returned to reconcile with his wife.

The definite article in (al-ʿiddah) is for a known reference, since the observance was legislated earlier, as you have known just now, and the statement is according to an implied omitted term, since what is counted is the days of the waiting period.

The addressees of the pronoun in (ahsu, "count") are the addressees of the pronoun in (idha tallaqtum, "when you divorce"). So each person to whom this ruling relates takes his share: the divorcer, the divorced woman, and whoever becomes aware of a violation of this among the Muslims, especially the rulers, judges, and those responsible for public accountability (ahl al-hisbah), for they are most entitled to upholding Allah's laws in the community, especially when they see the spread of disregard for what the Sharia intends. We have explained this in the chapter on the objectives of the judiciary in my book "Maqasid al-Shari'ah."

So in the waiting period there are many benefits, and beneath them are various rights, which these many benefits require. Most of these rights belong to the divorcer and the divorced woman, and they entail rights for the Muslims and their rulers in safeguarding those rights, especially when litigation arises.

* * *

﴿And fear Allah, your Lord﴾.

A parenthetical insertion between the clause ﴿and count the waiting period﴾ and the clause ﴿do not expel them from their houses﴾. The waw is parenthetical.

The object of (ittaqu Allah, "fear Allah") is omitted so that it encompasses everything in which Allah is to be feared. This is therefore of the kind of the concluding parenthetical insertion, and the first thing intended by fearing Allah in it is what the discourse was brought for.

So His saying (﴿and fear Allah, your Lord﴾) is a warning against laxity in the rulings of divorce and the waiting period. That is because the people of ignorance did not give women any weight, and the relatives of divorced women rarely defended them, so people neglected those rights and disregarded them. Therefore these verses were

severe in tone in their challenge, and those rights were expressed by taqwa and by the limits of Allah. To increase the emphasis on taqwa, the name of majesty was followed by the description "your Lord," as a reminder that He is worthy of being feared for His anger.

﴿Do not expel them from their houses, nor should they leave, except that they commit a clear immorality﴾.

It is a resumption, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of (ahsu al-ʿiddah), meaning: the waiting period being in their houses. It may also be a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the content of the clause "count the waiting period," since their staying in their houses during the waiting period realizes the meaning of counting the waiting period.

For both interpretations, the clause is detached from conjunction with the waw, and this is either permissible or obligatory.

The attribution of the houses to the women's pronoun implies that they deserve to remain in the houses for the duration of the 'iddah (the waiting period), in the position of the owner of a thing. In jurisprudence (fiqh) this is called the right of use without ownership of the property (milk al-intifa' dun al-'ayn). Also, the remaining of divorced women in the houses in which they were wives is a continuation of the state of marriage, since the wife is the one who manages her husband's house, and for this reason the Arabs call her "the mistress of the house" (rabbat al-bayt). A divorced woman has the ruling of a wife for as long as she is in the 'iddah, except regarding the husband's enjoyment of her.

The cause of this ruling is composed of the intention of kindness between the divorcing man and the divorced woman, and the intention of regulating the reason for the 'iddah, in order to complete the certainty that any pregnancy that appears is attached to its father, the divorcing man, so that lineage is cleared of all doubt.

The clause ﴿nor shall they leave﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Do not expel them﴾. It is a prohibition upon them from leaving, for the divorcing man may expel her, and then the divorced woman desires to leave, because she finds it burdensome to remain in a house from which her authority has departed. So God forbade them to leave. If the house is rented, the divorced woman lives in it, its rent is upon the divorcing man, and when the term of its rent ends, it is upon the divorcing man to renew it until the end of the divorced woman's 'iddah.

This sequence between the two clauses indicates causation, and that every woman in 'iddah has a right to residence in her husband's house for the duration of the 'iddah, because she is in 'iddah on account of him, that is, for the sake of preserving his lineage and honour. This is what the verse requires. For this reason Malik and the majority of scholars held that residence is obligatory for the divorced woman who has been consummated with, whether the divorce was revocable (raj'i) or irrevocable (ba'in). Ibn Abi Layla said: there is no residence except for the revocably divorced woman. He gave several reasons for the obligation of residence for the consummated divorced woman: preserving lineage, consoling the divorced woman, and preserving her honour. Later in this surah God, exalted is He, will say ﴿Lodge them where you dwell﴾ [al-Talaq: 6], and you know that this is an affirmation of what is in this verse of the obligation of residence during the 'iddah. It was repeated in order to explain upon it His words ﴿according to your means﴾ [al-Talaq: 6] and what is conjoined to it.

The exception in His words ﴿unless they commit a flagrant indecency﴾ may refer to the two clauses preceding it, as is the case when it comes after several clauses according to the most correct opinion of the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). It may also refer to the last of them, and this is what is required by its agreement with the pronoun, since the pronoun in both of them is the pronoun of the women. It is an exception from the generality of circumstances that the generality of the persons implies in His words ﴿Do not expel them﴾ and ﴿nor shall they leave﴾. So the meaning is: "unless they commit an indecency, then expel them", or "let them leave", meaning it is permitted for you to expel them, and they have no right to refuse to leave; and likewise the reverse.

The fahisha (indecency) is the extremely evil act, and by this its use in the common usage of the language became prevalent, so it includes fornication, as in His words ﴿And those of your women who commit indecency﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], the verse in Surat al-Nisa'.

It also includes other works of corruption, as in His words ﴿And when they commit an indecency, they say: "We found our fathers doing it"﴾ [al-A'raf: 28], and His words ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾ [al-A'raf: 33], in Surat al-A'raf. Ibn 'Atiyya said: some people said: "Whenever fahisha appears in the Qur'an in the definite form, it means fornication" (he means or what resembles it), as in His words ﴿Do you commit the indecency that no one among the worlds has committed before you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 80]. And whenever it appears indefinite, it means sins.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read ﴿mubayyinah﴾ with a kasra on the ya' (i.e., "making clear"), meaning that it makes clear to whoever reaches it that it is a great indecency. Attributing the making-clear to it is then a metaphor, by the figurative use of "making clear" for "being evident". Or it means that it makes clear to the authorities that it came from the woman, so the attribution of making-clear to the indecency is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), and the one who makes it clear is actually the one involved in it, namely the confession and the testimony. So in each case it is understood in the sense that suits the meaning of "making clear".

Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read ﴿mubayyinah﴾ with a fatha on the ya' (i.e., "proven"), meaning that it was an indecency which proof made evident, or which an outsider made evident. The basis of the two readings is one.

Describing it as "mubayyinah" may mean that it is evident within the category of indecencies, i.e., it is a great indecency, and this context implies that its greatness is the greatness of what women customarily commit of such things. It may also mean that it is evident in its establishment for the period in which she leaves.

Scholars have differed about the intended meaning of fahisha here and about the meaning of leaving because of it. From Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Dahhak, 'Ikrima, Hammad, al-Layth ibn Sa'd and Abu Yusuf: that the fahisha is fornication. They said: the purpose of the exception is permission to expel them, i.e., so that the legal punishment (hadd) may be applied to them.

Fahisha was interpreted as abusive speech against the neighbours and the in-laws, or against the husband, such that the continued presence of such women in the household of the family leads to repeated quarrels, so expelling her is the choice of the lesser of two harms. This was attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, because he read ﴿unless they abuse you (yafhashna 'alaykum)﴾ with a ya' with a fatha and a dammah on the unmarked ha' (meaning "transgression by foul speech"). It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and was chosen by al-Shafi'i.

Fahisha was interpreted as disobedience, such as theft, insult, or leaving the house, for the 'iddah itself, let alone fornication. This was attributed to Ibn 'Abbas as well, and Ibn 'Umar, and it was said by al-Suddi and Abu Hanifa.

From Qatada: fahisha is nushuz (disobedience/rebellion), i.e., if he divorced her because of her nushuz, then she has no residence.

From Ibn 'Umar and al-Suddi: the exception is referred back to the clause to which it is attached, which is the clause ﴿nor shall they leave﴾. That is, they are forbidden to leave except if they wish to commit an indecency. The meaning of this is the desire to make the act of their leaving abominable: that is, if they wish to commit an indecency, they may leave. This is by what is called "affirming a thing by what resembles its opposite", which al-Sakkaki named, in the terminology of the earlier scholars, "affirming the one who praises by what resembles blame". Among its examples is the words of al-Nabigha:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords
are notched by them from the clashing of the battalions."

So the verse made their leaving a cause of suspicion for them, and warned women against it in a rhetorical style, with the kha' vowelled with a fatha (i.e., "the one who is addressed" in a rhetorical sense). So this exception is a prohibition upon them from leaving by way of emphasis in the forbidding.

The verb ﴿they commit﴾ (ya'tina) on this interpretation is understood as "those who wish to commit", like ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6].

It has been related in the Sahih (of Muslim): from the Prophet ﷺ, that Fatima bint Qays al-Fihriyya came to him and informed him that her husband, Abu 'Amr ibn Hafs or Abu Hafs ibn 'Amr, whom the Prophet ﷺ had sent with 'Ali to Yemen, sent her from Yemen a single divorce, which coincided with the last of the three, so she became irrevocably separated from him. He also sent to some of his relatives that they should provide maintenance for her during the 'iddah, but they said to her: "You have no maintenance unless you are pregnant." She brought her matter to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "You have no maintenance." She asked his permission to move, so he permitted her to observe the 'iddah in the house of Ibn Umm Maktum. In another narration: "She said: I fear that someone will break in upon me" (in the passive form), and in another narration: "She was in a desolate, frightening place on her side, so the Prophet ﷺ ordered her to move."

The scholars differed about her moving. A group said: it is a concession (rukhsa) specific to Fatima bint Qays which does not go beyond her. 'A'isha, the Mother of the Believers, held this view. Al-Bukhari related that Yahya ibn Sa'id ibn al-'As divorced his wife 'Amra bint 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hakam, whose paternal uncle Marwan ibn al-Hakam was then governor of Medina. Her father moved her to him. This reached 'A'isha, the Mother of the Believers, and she sent to Marwan: "Fear God and return her to her house." Marwan said: "Has not the account of Fatima bint Qays reached you?" 'A'isha said: "It does not harm you that you do not mention the hadith of Fatima." Marwan said: "If there is evil in you, then what lies between these two of evil is enough for you." Perhaps 'A'isha was satisfied by this, since it is not reported that she replied to him.

In the Sahih it is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "We will not abandon the Book of God and the Sunna of our Prophet for the word of a woman, whom we do not know whether she remembered or forgot." 'A'isha said: "Fatima bint Qays has no report in mentioning this hadith," and she criticised her with the severest criticism. She said: "Fatima was in a desolate, frightening place on her side, so the Prophet ﷺ gave her a concession to move." It appears from this that there is a difference of opinion about the reality of the excuse which justifies moving. Malik said: "A woman may not move from the place of her 'iddah without an excuse." Related by al-Baji in al-Muntaqa.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: leaving because of a calamity, abuse, a need for livelihood, or fear of ruin from the dwelling is permitted by the Sunna.

Among the scholars there are those who permitted moving in cases of necessity, and they made this the interpretation of the hadith of Fatima bint Qays, for she feared for herself in a desolate place, and evil and abuse arose between her and her husband's family. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "That woman used to overpower her in-laws with her tongue; she was sharp-tongued, so the Messenger of God ﷺ ordered her to move." This difference is close to being a verbal difference, since all agree except 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that her moving was for an excuse which the Prophet ﷺ accepted. So that case specifies the verse, and analogy (qiyas) is applied to it when the effective cause (illa) of the analogy is established.

As for the statement of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, "We will not abandon the Book of God and the Sunna of our Prophet for the word of a woman, whether she remembered or forgot," it is a rejection of the report of Fatima bint Qays on the basis of doubt concerning her, so it does not oppose a verse, until one proceeds to reconcile them by specification (takhsis) and concession (tarkhis). Ibn al-'Arabi said: it has been said that 'Umar did not specify the Qur'an by a report of a single transmitter (khabar al-wahid).

As for defining the prohibition on the woman in 'iddah leaving her house, there is no disagreement that spending the night outside her house is forbidden. As for her leaving during the day to attend to her own affairs, Malik, al-Layth ibn Sa'd and Ahmad permitted it for the woman in 'iddah absolutely.

Al-Shafi'i said: the revocably divorced woman does not leave, neither by night nor by day, while the irrevocably divorced woman leaves by day. Abu Hanifa said: the woman in 'iddah of death may leave by day, and no other may leave, neither by night nor by day.

In the Sahih of Muslim: Marwan ibn al-Hakam sent to Fatima bint Qays asking her about her hadith. When it was reported to him, he said: "We have not heard this hadith except from a woman; we will hold to the protection upon which we found the people." Fatima, when the words of Marwan reached her, said: "Then between me and you is the Qur'an." God, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Do not expel them from their houses, nor shall they leave, unless they commit a flagrant indecency. These are the limits of God, and whoever transgresses the limits of God has wronged himself. You do not know; perhaps God will bring about after that some matter﴾. This is for the one who has the right of return. So what matter will arise after the three? How then can you say: "She has no maintenance if she is not pregnant"? For what do you detain her? She thought that remaining in her house was for maintaining the connection between her and the one who divorced her, and that she was obliged to it for the sake of maintenance.

The wisdom in the residence (sukna) of the divorced woman that has become clear to me is the preservation of honour (hifz al-a'rad). A divorced woman attracts many eyes, ill suspicion may creep toward her, she faces much contention, and she has no protector (dhu 'ismah) to defend her. For this reason the residence was prescribed for her, and she may not leave except for her necessary needs. This is a wisdom of the type of likelihood (maznnah). Hence, if circumstances arise that place her in hardship, or that place people in hardship because of her, she is removed from that dwelling, and what applies to her staying in the dwelling to which she moves is what applies to her in the dwelling of her divorcer, because the likelihood (maznnah) has been opposed by a certainty (ma'innah). Also among the ruling in this matter is that the divorced woman may not find a dwelling, since most women have no property and are dependents upon men. Since the woman in 'idda was prohibited from marrying, providing her residence became a right upon the one who separated from her, by way of maintaining the status quo (istis-hab al-hal), until she becomes lawful for marriage, whereupon her residence falls upon whoever marries her. And in the case of the revocable divorcee (raj'iyyah), there is added the purpose of preserving the bond between her and her divorcer, perhaps his sound judgment will return to him and he will take her back, so that he does not need to repeat the arrangements between him and her or between him and her family. This is a collection of causes (ʿilal). If one of them is absent, the ruling is not absent, because a ruling founded on two causes or more is not nullified by the falling away of some of them, unlike a compound cause when one part of it is absent.

﴿And these are the limits of Allah﴾. The waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), and the sentence is interposed between the clause (﴿and they shall not go out﴾) and the clause (﴿You know not, perhaps Allah will bring about after that some matter﴾). By this interposition is intended to hasten the alert to the establishment of the rulings mentioned from the beginning of the surah, establishing them without negligence, and no one has the option of leniency in them, especially the divorced woman and the divorcer, lest they suppose that this is their right, individually or jointly.
The pointing (ishara) to the preceding sentences is in terms of their meanings, by interpreting them as matters (bi-ta'wil al-qada'a).
Hudud is the plural of hadd, which is that which restrains (yahuddu), i.e., prevents from passing beyond it into the places they do not like to enter, either absolutely, like the boundaries of a protected preserve (hima), or because of the obligation to change a state, like the boundaries of the sacred precinct (haram) prohibiting hunting, and the boundaries of the stations (mawaqit) for entering ihram for hajj and 'umrah.
The meaning: these rulings resemble the limits in being guarded in what they require in this respect.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 65, verse 2:

﴿Then when they reach their term, retain them in good fellowship or part from them in good fellowship.﴾

This is a derivation (tafri') from all the preceding rulings on the waiting period ('iddah), coordinated with the phrase (﴿And count the waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]), because counting it means preserving its duration and encompassing its days. When the period has ended, God has excused both of them, and any extension beyond it is harm to one of them or to both. The benefit of the fixed terms is to halt at their conclusion.

The original sense of reaching a term (bulugh al-ajal) is the end of the period specified for it, as the meaning of "bulugh," which is arrival at the goal, indicates. This is by way of likening a specified term to a place one travels toward, and this usage became common. So the figurative usage lies in the word ajal (term), and "reaching" follows it as a figurative usage. In this verse, "reaching" is used to mean approaching that end, for the sake of emphasis on not being lenient about it. This usage is another figure, by way of the resemblance of approaching a thing to attaining it and being engaged in it.

The indicator (qarinah) of the figure here is the word ajal, because return (muraja'ah) cannot be conceived after the term has been reached, since that would negate the meaning of the deferral (ta'jil).

From the same is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term, retain them in good fellowship or release them in good fellowship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Page 308

And "retention" (imsak) is the resolve to return, expressed by the word imsak as a hint that a revocable divorcee has the ruling of a wife in all respects except sexual enjoyment. So it is as if, when he has taken her back, he has retained her so that she does not leave him, and so it is as if he had not parted from her, because imsak is holding on to a thing and not being negligent with it. From the same is the Exalted's saying: (﴿Keep your wife to yourself﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]). And if he does not return to her, it is as if he has renewed the separation and his heart has hardened.

For this subtle point, not retaining is made a new separation in His saying: (﴿or part from them in good fellowship﴾).

The command in (﴿retain them﴾) or (﴿part from them﴾) is for permission (ibahah), and the "or" in it is for choice (takhyir).

The ba' in ﴿in good fellowship﴾ is for accompaniment (mulabasah), meaning that each of retention and parting is accompanied by what is good (ma'ruf).

The ma'ruf is what husbands have customarily recognized as good treatment in companionship and in parting.

So the ma'ruf in retention is: good meeting, apologizing to her for what was neglected, and returning to good companionship.

The ma'ruf in parting is: restraining the tongue from backbiting her and showing relief from her.

The ma'ruf in both states is the man's action, because he is the one addressed with retaining or parting.

As for the ma'ruf that is the woman's action, it is established by other proofs, such as the Exalted's saying: (﴿And they have rights similar to their obligations, according to what is ma'ruf﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228]).

Placing retention, meaning return, before carrying out separation indicates that it is more pleasing to God, the Exalted, and more in accordance with the aims of the Shari'ah. Together with the earlier expression of return as retention, it is understood that return is recommended, because the most hated of permissible things to God is divorce.

Since the command of permission in (﴿retain them﴾) or (﴿part from them﴾) is restricted by the qualifier "in good fellowship," it is understood that if retention is not in good fellowship, it is not permitted. This is the retention that people of the Jahiliyyah used to practice: a man would divorce his wife, and when she approached the end of her waiting period he would take her back for some days, then divorce her again, doing this three times in order to prolong the waiting period over her, so that she would not marry for months, as harm to her.

This was already mentioned at his saying: (﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]), up to his saying (﴿And do not retain them to harm them, transgressing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]), in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿And call to witness two just men from among you.﴾

The apparent placement of this command after mention of retention or parting indicates that it refers to both, because witnessing is made a completion of what is commanded, in the sense of a condition for retention or parting, since this coordination resembles a qualifier even though it is not one. The nature of conditions that come after a series of clauses is that they apply to all of them.

The apparent form of the imperative indicates obligation. From these two points it follows that witnessing both the return and the final pronouncement of divorce is obligatory upon the spouses, because witnessing removes many kinds of disputes. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and it was adopted by Yahya ibn Bukayr of the Malikis, al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions, and Ibn Hanbal in one of his two opinions. It is also reported from 'Imran ibn Husayn, Tawus, Ibrahim, Abu Qilabah, and 'Ata'. The majority said: the witnessing commanded is witnessing of the return, not of the final pronouncement of divorce.

As for what the form of the command in the Exalted's saying {﴿And call to witness two just men﴾} requires, it has been said that it is recommended (mustahabb). This is the view of Abu Hanifah, and the well-known view of Malik as transmitted by Ibn al-Qassar. Perhaps the basis of this view is that the practice of obligating it did not operate among Muslims in the age of the Companions and the ages of the scholars, and that it is analogized to witnessing in sale, on which they agreed that it is not obligatory. Both of these are flawed: the claim of a practice of abandoning witnessing is a disputed claim, and analogizing divorce and return to sale may be challenged by a relevant difference, namely the danger of divorce and return and the gravity of what follows from them of disputes among lineages, which is not present in sales, where exchange of consideration itself suffices without witnessing. It has also been said that the command is obligatory with respect to return and not separation; this is one of al-Shafi'i's two views and Ahmad's, and Isma'il ibn Hammad, one of the Maliki jurists of Baghdad, attributed it to Malik, and it is the apparent position of Ibn Bukayr's school.

All agree that this witnessing is not a condition for the validity of return or parting, because it was legislated only as a precaution for the rights of both and to avoid disputes, fearing that if one dies the other claims she was not divorced, or that she dies and he claims so. It seems they based this on the view that a command does not require immediacy. Moreover, making one thing a condition for another requires specific evidence other than the evidence of obligation, because the sin may be incurred by abandoning it without invalidating what it was commanded to accompany, like prayer in a usurped land or in a usurped garment.

Those who hold witnessing obligatory said: if he returned without witnessing, or pronounced separation without witnessing, his return and separation are valid, and he must call witnesses afterward.

Yahya ibn Bukayr said: the meaning of witnessing the return and separation is that he calls witnesses at her return if he returns to her, and at the end of her waiting period if he does not return to her, that he had divorced her and that her waiting period has ended.

Among the jurists of the regions there are detailed differences about what constitutes return, whether by verbal formula or by an act of the kind done by husbands. Their details belong in the books of furu'. Nothing from them relates to the verse except what the people of knowledge took as evidence for return according to those who so take it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 65, verse 3:

﴿Whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him. Indeed, Allah accomplishes His command.﴾

This is a complement to the preceding verse, for taqwa of Allah (fear and awareness of Allah, God-consciousness) is the means of relief from distress and deliverance from straits. The Muslim's awareness of this and his certainty that Allah repels from him the satanic thoughts that come to his mind and that discourage him from taqwa, and that Allah fulfils His promise to him by making for him a way out and providing for him from where he does not expect.

*Hasb* (sufficient): an adjective meaning "sufficient" (*kafin*). Its origin is either an infinitive noun (*ism masdar*) or a verbal noun (*masdar*).

[p. 313]

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah accomplishes His command﴾ is in the position of the cause (*'illa*) for the clause ﴿Whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him﴾. That is, do not consider unlikely the occurrence of what Allah has promised you when you see that its causes are absent, for when Allah promises a promise, He has willed it, and when Allah wills a matter, He facilitates its causes.

Perhaps His saying ﴿Allah has set a measure for everything﴾ alludes to this meaning: Allah knows that He will suffice whoever relies upon Him in his affair, so He has decreed its causes just as He has decreed the causes of all things. So do not doubt the fulfilment of His promise, for when He wills a matter, He facilitates its causes in ways that people do not reckon, and the workings of Allah the Exalted are hidden and wondrous.

The meaning of ﴿accomplishes His command﴾: reaches His intended goal. "Reaching" (*bulugh*) is a well-known metaphor for attaining what is desired. And "command" (*amr*) here means "affair" (*sha'n*).

It is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Rafi' that when His saying ﴿Whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him﴾ was revealed, some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "So when we rely upon Allah, we let go of what we have and do not guard it." Then ﴿Indeed, Allah accomplishes His command﴾ was revealed, meaning: concerning you and against you. End of quote.

Qara'a al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read *bali'un* with tanwin and *amrahu* in the accusative. Hafs, from 'Asim, read *bali'u amrihi* with *bali'* in the genitive construction (idafa) to *amrihi*.
