﴿Allah has set a measure for everything﴾.

This clause has a position in which a feature of the inimitability (*i'jaz*) of the Qur'an appears in the arrangement of its clauses, one after another, as I have pointed out in earlier passages. This clause occupies the position of a *istinaf bayani* (explanatory resumption), arising from what the clauses ﴿Whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2] up to His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah accomplishes His command﴾ contain. This is because the readiness of the listeners to be certain of what those clauses contain varies. Some listeners may find it unlikely that such a promise will be fulfilled for people like them, given the disorder of their circumstances as those clauses present it, or their certainty may waver, so they say: "Where am I from attaining this?" when they look and see a great distance from the attainment of what was promised, because the means to it are absent for them, and despair overtakes them.

[p. 314]

This explanatory resumption came after the promise as a reminder that Allah knows His promises and has prepared the measures for their fulfilment, because He has set a measure for everything.

This clause also has the position of a causal justification (*ta'lil*) for the clause ﴿and count the waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1], for the waiting period is among the things. When Allah commanded that its term be counted, He justified that by saying that Allah has made the measure of the duration of the waiting period, so there is no permission to be negligent about it.

It also has the position of a concluding summary (*tadhyil*) for the clause ﴿Those are the limits of Allah, and whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has wronged himself﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]; that is, He who set those limits has set a measure for everything that cannot be exceeded, just as He set the limits.

It also has the position of a causal justification for the clause ﴿So when they have reached their term, either retain them in kindness or part from them in kindness﴾ [al-Talaq: 2], because the meaning is: when they have reached the measure that Allah set for the duration of the waiting period, then the legal purpose indicated by His saying ﴿You do not know; perhaps Allah will bring about after that some matter﴾ [al-Talaq: 1] has been achieved. The meaning is: if Allah does not bring about the matter of reconciliation, then He has been gentle with you and has removed from you the prolongation of the waiting period.

It also has the position of a causal justification for the clause ﴿And establish testimony for Allah﴾ [al-Talaq: 2], for Allah has made testimony a measure for ending disputes.

This clause is part of a verse, and it contains realities of wisdom.

The meaning of ﴿for everything﴾ is: for every existing thing, that is, for every occurrence. The existing thing, whether it is a substance or one of the meanings, is included. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And everything they have done is in the scriptures﴾ [al-Qamar: 52]. So the generality of His saying ﴿for everything﴾ is explicit that what Allah has promised has, at the time of its coming into being, a measure assigned to it.

Al-Raghib said in his *Mufradat*: "That is because the act of Allah is of two kinds. One kind He brought into existence actually; the meaning of bringing it into existence actually is that He originated it complete at once, not subject to increase or decrease, until He wills to make it perish or change it, like the heavens and what is in them. And among them is that which He made its roots existent in actuality and its parts potential, and He measured it in a way that from it can come only what He measured in it, like His measuring in the date-stone that from it a palm tree grows, not an apple or an olive tree, and His measuring in the human sperm that from it a human is produced and not another animal. So Allah's measuring is in two ways: one of them is by His ruling that a thing shall be such or shall not be such, either by way of necessity or by way of possibility; and to this belongs His saying ﴿Allah has set a measure for everything﴾. The second is by giving the capacity for it, and to this belongs His saying ﴿So We measured, and how excellent are the measurers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 23], or it may be of the kind of His saying ﴿Allah has set a measure for everything﴾." End of quote.

*Al-qadr*: the verbal noun of *qadara* (transitive to an object), with the *dal* lightened, meaning to place in something a measure of quantity, whether intrinsic or abstract, that is set according to what the object can bear. So the measure of every object of an action is the measure its capacity and ability can bear of works, or what its extent can bear of things, or what its understanding can bear of perceptions and comprehensions that its mind strains to grasp. Among the branches of this meaning is what is in His saying ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying here ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond what He has given it﴾ [al-Talaq: 7].

Among the particular instances of the meaning of *qadr* is what is called *taqdir*, the verbal noun of *qaddara* (the doubled form), when one makes a thing or things to a specific measure suited to the purpose for which it was made, as in His saying ﴿And measure well in the link-up﴾ [Saba': 11] in Surat Saba'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 65, verses 4–5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And for those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months, and likewise for those who have not menstruated.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with His saying (﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]), for the waiting period there (ʿiddah) refers to menstrual cycles (aqrāʾ). That implies that the woman in this waiting period is one who has menstrual cycles. Thus there remains the explanation of the waiting period of the woman who has passed the age of menstruation, or the one who has not reached the age of those who menstruate, namely the young girl. Both of them are truly described as having despaired of menstruation, that is, at that time.

The pause (waqf) is at His saying (﴿and likewise for those who have not menstruated﴾), meaning that they are coordinated with those who have despaired.

Yaʾs (despair) is the absence of hope. What is despaired of in the verse is known from the context, from His saying (﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]), that is, they have despaired of menstruation, whether that despair comes after it has occurred repeatedly or because it has not appeared, meaning it has not stopped due to illness or breastfeeding. The age for this varies according to the individual and the region, just as the age at which menstruation begins varies. The determination of this age has been disputed by number of years. It was said: sixty years; and it was said: fifty-five. Leaving it unspecified by years is better, and this is only an approximation of the time of despair.

The purpose of the verse is clear, and it particularizes (takhsīs) the generality of His saying (﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228]) in Surat al-Baqarah. Surat al-Ṭalāq was revealed after Surat al-Baqarah.

The implication of the condition in His saying (﴿if you are in doubt﴾) and what is connected to it has been obscured. Most of the exegetes (ahl al-tafsīr) took this condition as connected to the statement in which it occurs, and that it is not connected to His saying (﴿Do not turn them out of their houses﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]) at the beginning of this surah, contrary to an eccentric and far-fetched interpretation that scatters the unity of the speech. Then the meaning of this condition was obscured by His saying (﴿if you are in doubt﴾).

Scholars have two approaches to this. The first approach: its proponents held that the referent of despair is not the referent of doubt, because the object of each differs. Ashhab related from Malik that when God, exalted is He, explained the waiting period of women who have menstrual cycles and women who are pregnant, that is, in Surat al-Baqarah, the despairing women and those who had not menstruated remained, and the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ were in doubt about their matter, so this verse was revealed. A similar report is transmitted from Mujahid. Al-Ṭabarī related a report: "From Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, that he asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the waiting period of these two, who were not mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, and this verse was revealed." They took the particle (in) to mean (idh) (when), and that the doubt occurred regarding the ruling on the waiting period before the revelation of the verse, that is: when you were in doubt about the ruling on that, we explained it by this verse. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "The hadith of Ubayy is not authentic." I say: It was related by al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan, and al-Ḥākim in al-Mustadrak, and he authenticated it. And al-Ṭabarānī with its chain from ʿAmr ibn Sālim, that Ubayy said. There is nothing in al-Ṭabarī's narration that indicates the chain of the hadith.

It is in al-Bayhaqī's narration with its chain to Abū ʿUthmān ʿUmar ibn Sālim al-Anṣārī, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and it is discontinuous (munqaṭiʿ), because Abū ʿUthmān did not meet Ubayy ibn Kaʿb. I suppose that it is also so in al-Ḥākim's Mustadrak, because al-Bayhaqī narrated it from al-Ḥākim. So there is no basis for Ibn al-ʿArabī's statement that it is not authentic, for the men in its chain are trustworthy (thiqāt).

In Asbāb al-Nuzūl of al-Wāḥidī, from Qatādah: "That Khallād ibn al-Nuʿmān and Ubayy asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about that, and this verse was revealed." It was said that the questioner was Muʿādh ibn Jabal, who asked about the waiting period of the woman who has despaired.

So the doubt on this approach means the uncertainty that arose regarding the ruling on these divorced women. Thus the conditional clause is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍ) between the subject, which is the relative pronoun, and its predicate, which is the clause (﴿their waiting period is three months﴾).

The fāʾ in (﴿fa-ʿiddatuhunna﴾) is attached to the predicate clause because the relative pronoun carries the meaning of a condition, like His saying (﴿And those two of you who commit it, harm them﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 16]), and similar examples are numerous in speech.

Doubt on this approach has already occurred in the past, so (in) is used in the sense of certainty without any special purpose.

The second approach: its proponents held that the referent of despair and the referent of doubt are one and the same, namely the state of the divorced woman with regard to menstruation. This is from ʿIkrimah, Qatādah and Ibn Zayd, and Yaḥyā ibn Bukayr and Ismāʿīl ibn Hād of the Mālikīs interpreted it this way, and Ibn Lubābah of the Mālikīs attributed it to Dāwūd al-Ẓāhirī.

This interpretation makes it clear that the meaning of doubt is the occurrence of uncertainty regarding the woman's condition.

On this basis, the conditional clause and its response is a statement about (﴿those who have despaired﴾), that is: if they (the women) are in doubt, and you (men) are in doubt because of their doubt. The masculine plural pronoun of addressees is then used with precedence (taghlīb), and the condition remains a condition. Doubt here is in the future, and the fāʾ is the linking particle of the response.

This interpretation implies that the waiting of three months is conditional on the occurrence of doubt about their despair of menstruation. Hence its proponents collided with the concept of the condition (mafhūm al-sharṭ), which implies that if doubt does not occur about their despair, they do not observe that waiting period, or they do not observe any waiting period at all. Ibn Lubābah, one of the Mālikī jurists, attributed to Dāwūd al-Ẓāhirī that he held the waiting period falls away for the woman whose despair is certain.

I say: this attribution to Dāwūd is not known. Ibn Ḥazm did not report it from him, nor did anyone who addressed the differences of the jurists report it. Ibn Lubābah said: "This is an anomaly (shudhūdh)." Ibn Lubābah also said: "As for Ibn Bukayr and Ismāʿīl ibn Ḥammād," that is, of the Mālikī jurists, "they made the woman whose despair is certain analogous to the doubtful woman in the waiting period by way of analogy (qiyās)," meaning that the waiting period has two wisdoms: the clearing of the womb, and the waiting for reconciliation. As for those who do not regard the concept of opposition (mafhūm al-mukhālafa), they are free of what binds those who regard it.

The proponents of this approach differ in the direction and in how the verse is to be understood accordingly. ʿIkrimah, Ibn Zayd and Qatādah said: the woman who is in doubt about the return of menstruation to her has no waiting period longer than three months, clinging to the apparent meaning of the verse. Probably the reason for this view is that within three months the matter of pregnancy becomes clear; if no pregnancy appears after it ends, the woman's waiting period is complete, because pregnancy after the age of despair is rare. But if doubt about pregnancy arises, the question shifts to the ruling on doubt about pregnancy, and that is a different issue from the one the verse was revealed about.

Most scholars said: the doubtful woman in her despair remains for nine months (that is, the usual period of pregnancy). If no pregnancy appears in her, she begins the waiting period of three months, so that she completes a full year. The basis of this is what Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab related from the judgment of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, and no one among the Companions disagreed, and Mālik adopted it. And from Mālik in al-Mudawwana: nine months for doubt, and the three months are the waiting period. Probably they regarded the waiting period after the passing of the nine months as a devotional matter (taʿabbud), because that is what is in the Qur'an. As for the nine months, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb made them obligatory, probably by ijtihād (independent reasoning), and it is a restriction (taqyīd) of the unrestricted generality found in the verse.

Al-Nakhaʿī, Sufyān al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī said: the doubtful woman in her despair observes the waiting period by menstrual cycles, that is, she waits for blood until she reaches the age of one who is not likely to menstruate, even if the period of her waiting exceeds nine months. When she reaches the age of despair without doubt, she observes a waiting period of three months from that day. We interpret their view by holding that the sense of the speech is: "their waiting period is three months," that is, after the cessation of doubt, as we shall mention. Yet this still implies that these three months after the passing of nine months, or after the passing of a period that brings her to the age of one who is not likely to menstruate, is a devotional matter, because the absence of pregnancy has become clear and the waiting for reconciliation has been prolonged. Unless we excuse them by saying that during the waiting period the divorcer is not yet moved to decide about reconciliation, since he is within the scope of waiting, and so the period is extended for that reason. In the tafsir of al-Qurṭubī: ʿIkrimah and Qatādah said: "Among the doubtful is the woman who has irregular bleeding, whose menstruation does not follow a regular pattern, sometimes at the beginning of the month, several times, and sometimes once in months," that is, without regularity. Al-Ṭabarī related similar words from al-Zuhrī and Ibn Zayd. So this aspect must be adopted in interpreting the verse. When a woman approaches the time of despair, menstruation does not cease from her all at once, but she remains for months with menstruation coming at intervals without regularity, until it ends entirely.

His saying (﴿and likewise for those who have not menstruated﴾) is coordinated with (﴿and those who have despaired﴾), and the implied sense is: "their waiting period is three months." It is good to pause at His saying (﴿their waiting period is three months﴾).

* * *

﴿And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they deliver their burden.﴾

It is coordinated with the clause (﴿and likewise for those who have not menstruated﴾). It completes the states of the waiting period, which were stated in summary in His saying (﴿and count the waiting period﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]). The implied sense is: (﴿and for those pregnant among them﴾), that is, among the divorced women, their term is until they deliver their burden.

Thus through this verse together with the preceding one, the states of the divorced women are detailed, and an explanation is also given of the summary in the verse in Surat al-Baqarah.

(﴿Ulāt﴾) is a plural noun meaning: those possessing. (Dhāt) is the feminine of (dhū), meaning: possessor. There is no singular of (ulāt) from its own form, just as there is no singular of the word (ulū), and (ulāt) is like (dhawāt), just as (ulū) is like (dhawū). (Ulāt) is written in the orthography with a waw after the hamza, following the spelling of the word (ulū) with a waw after the hamza, in order to distinguish in writing between (ulī) in the accusative and genitive cases and the preposition (ilā). I wish they had restricted this spelling with a waw after the hamza to the word (ulī) in the masculine accusative or genitive, and left aside the artificial spelling in other cases.

The waiting period of a divorced pregnant woman is ended by the delivery of the child, because nothing more clearly indicates the clearing of the womb, since the primary purpose of the waiting period is to establish the clearing of the womb of a child of the divorcer, or to make evident that the womb is occupied with a fetus of his. Another purpose was added to this, namely to await the regret of the divorcer and to enable him to correct his matter by reconciliation. When the more important purpose was achieved, the rest were set aside, in consideration of the woman's right to be freed from the hardship of waiting. Moreover, pregnancy may occur close to the time of divorce, so the purpose of waiting was set aside, with the reasoning based on what is usual rather than what is rare. This is in contrast to those who said regarding the widow: "She must observe the longer of the two terms," which is attributed to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and Ibn ʿAbbās.

With this interpretation, this verse does not conflict with the verse on the waiting period of the widow in Surat al-Baqarah (﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234]), because that is in one valley and this is in another. That is about widows, and this is about divorced women.

However, since the term of four months and ten days for the widow has a wisdom limited to ensuring the clearing of the womb of the deceased husband's wife from a child of his, for there is no benefit in it other than that, and it should not be imagined that the Sharīʿah prescribed it for the purpose of grieving for the deceased husband, since it is definitively established that this is a pre-Islamic aim, and the Sharīʿah in many places has nullified it and forbidden it in many forms, as we have explained in the commentary on His saying (﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234]) etc. in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 65, verses 4–5 (part 2 of 2):

We have already known that the delivery of the child is the terminal point for the achievement of this purpose. It follows from the meaning that a pregnant widow, when she delivers her child, exits the waiting period of widowhood and does not need to complete four months and ten days, just as, if the duration of her pregnancy exceeded four months and ten days, she would not be confined to the four months and ten days, since there is no wisdom in that.

On account of this, the verse indicates that the waiting period of a pregnant woman is the delivery of her child, whether she is observing a waiting period due to divorce or a waiting period due to death.

On account of this, the majority of the scholars (ahl al-'ilm), from the Companions onward, said: the waiting period of a pregnant widow is like her waiting period due to divorce, namely the delivery of her child. However, their statements indicate that among them were those who, in a conflict between two general (ʿumūm) texts, held that the later of the two general texts abrogates the other general text, and this is the method of the earlier scholars (al-mutaqaddimīn).

The people of the authentic collections (ahl al-Ṣaḥīḥ) narrated that 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, when it reached him that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib had said concerning the waiting period of a pregnant widow that she must observe the longer of the two terms (i.e., the term of delivering the child and the term of four months and ten days), said: "The shorter sura of women (i.e., the sura of Divorce) was revealed after the longer one (i.e., after the longest of the suras), which is al-Baqara." That is, the verse of al-Baqara does not abrogate what is in the verse of the sura of Divorce.

(And there supports them the report of Subay'a bint al-Harith al-Aslamiyya, whose husband Sa'd ibn Khawla died during the Farewell Pilgrimage in Makka and left her pregnant; she delivered [her child] fifteen nights after his death, and it was said forty nights. She asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for permission to remarry, and he said to her: "You have become free [of the waiting period]; marry if you wish." Umm Salama, the Mother of the Believers, narrated it, and most of the Companions who came to know of it accepted it. The jurists after them received it with acceptance, and it is witnessed to by its meaning and wisdom, as has been mentioned just above.)

The later scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (ahl al-Usul) differed regarding the manner of acting in a conflict between two general texts, each of which is general in one respect, like these two verses. The majority adopted the preference of one of them by means of a preponderating factor, while the Hanafis held that the later of the two general texts abrogates the earlier one. So His saying (﴿And those who are pregnant [have as their term] until they deliver their burdens﴾) — because the relative pronoun is among the forms of generality, it encompasses every pregnant woman observing a waiting period, whether it is a waiting period due to divorce or a waiting period due to death. And His saying (﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind—they [the wives] shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]) encompasses every woman whom the deceased left behind, whether pregnant or not pregnant, because (﴿wives﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]) is an indefinite noun that occurs as the object of the relative clause, and (﴿they leave behind﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]), which contains the pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun which is general, so its object follows it in its generality, and thus it includes the widows who are pregnant, who are among those encompassed by the generality of (﴿And those who are pregnant﴾). Thus the two generalities conflict, each in one respect. The verse (﴿And those who are pregnant﴾) requires that all pregnant women's waiting period ends with delivery, and it may be that delivery occurs before the four months and ten days; while the verse of al-Baqara, by its generality, requires that widows wait four months and ten days, and this term may extend beyond the delivery of the child.

The majority went to preferring the generality of (﴿And those who are pregnant﴾) over the generality of (﴿and leave wives behind﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]) for several reasons.

The first: the generality of (﴿And those who are pregnant﴾) arises from the very wording itself, because the relative pronoun together with its clause is among the forms of generality. As for His saying (﴿and leave wives behind﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]), (﴿wives﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]) is an indefinite noun in an affirmative context, so it has no generality in its own wording; generality came to it only incidentally, following the generality of the governing relative pronoun. That which is general by its essence is stronger than that which is general by accident.

The second: the ruling in the generality of (﴿And those who are pregnant﴾) is attached to the meaning of the relative clause, which is a derivative, and attaching a ruling to a derivative indicates the causal basis of that from which it is derived. Unlike the generality in the sura of al-Baqara, the generality whose ruling is causally linked to an attribute is stronger in application than the generality whose ruling is not causally linked.

The third: the judgment of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning the waiting period of Subay'a al-Aslamiyya.

The Hanafis went to the view that the generality of (﴿And those who are pregnant﴾) abrogates the generality of His saying (﴿and leave wives behind﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]) to the extent to which the two conflicted.

The outcome of the two opinions is one: the waiting period of a pregnant woman is the delivery of her child, whether she is observing a waiting period due to divorce or due to the death of her husband.

The correct view is that the ruling of the verse of al-Baqara has not been lifted, and those who held that a widow who is not pregnant, if she delivers her child, must still observe a waiting period of four months and ten days are anomalous.

A few scholars held that the two verses should be reconciled in a way that realises the implementation of both together. They obligated the pregnant widow to observe the longer of the two terms: the term of four months and ten days and the term of delivering the child. This is the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas. Their aim in this is precaution, since the conflict here concerns the measure of two periods of time, so it was possible to act upon the wider of the two, which contains the other and something more. The meaning of this verse thus becomes: (﴿And those who are pregnant—their term is that they deliver their burden﴾) provided they are not in a waiting period due to death; and the meaning of the verse of al-Baqara becomes: and those widows whose husbands have died shall wait by themselves four months and ten days, provided they are not pregnant, for if they are pregnant they extend their waiting until delivery. And the generality of (﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind—they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]) is not to be specified by what is in the verse (﴿And those who are pregnant—their term is that they deliver their burden﴾) regarding the specificity concerning pregnant widows, since it is not permissible for the waiting period of a pregnant widow who has passed four months and ten days to end before she delivers her child, while she is still pregnant, because the invalidity of this is established by several proofs in the Sharia about which there is no disagreement. This is also the view of Ibn Abi Layla.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: "I was in a circle of notable Ansar" — that is, in Kufa — "and among them was 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, and his companions were admonishing him. He mentioned the later of the two terms, so I narrated the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba concerning the case of Subay'a bint al-Harith. 'Abd al-Rahman said: 'But his paternal uncle' — that is, the paternal uncle of 'Utba, who is 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud — 'did not used to say that' — that is, he did not narrate it to us. So I said: 'Then I would indeed be bold if I lied about a man on the outskirts of Kufa.' 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba was residing on the outskirts of Kufa. So I went out and met 'Amir or Malik ibn 'Awf, and I said: 'What was the statement of Ibn Mas'ud concerning a widow who is pregnant?' He said: 'Ibn Mas'ud said: "Do you impose the strictness upon her and not grant her the concession? The shorter sura of women was revealed after the longer one" (i.e., al-Baqara).'"

In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Abu Salama: a man came to Ibn 'Abbas while Abu Hurayra was sitting with him, and said: "Give me a ruling concerning a woman who gave birth forty nights after her husband." Ibn 'Abbas said: "The later of the two terms." I said: "(﴿And those who are pregnant—their term is that they deliver their burden﴾)." Abu Hurayra said: "I am with my nephew" — that is, with Abu Salama. Then Ibn 'Abbas sent Kurayb to Umm Salama to ask her, and she said: "He was killed" — (so it is said, though the verification is that he died during the Farewell Pilgrimage) — "the husband of Subay'a al-Aslamiyya, while she was pregnant, and she delivered forty nights after his death; then she was proposed to, and the Messenger of Allah married her off." Some have said that Ibn 'Abbas retracted his statement, but his retraction is not mentioned in the hadith of Abu Salama.

* * *

(﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him ease in his affair﴾) (﴿That is the command of Allah, which He has sent down to you; and whoever fears Allah, He will remove from him his misdeeds and enlarge for him a reward﴾).

This is a repetition of the admonition, and it is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad). What is said about it is the same as what is said about His saying, exalted is He (﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2] (﴿and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 3])). The purpose is to admonish men and women to adhere to what is in these rulings, which may involve hardship for someone, by way of obligating each to be patient in that in obedience to the command of Allah, for the one who complies, who is named the God-fearing (al-muttaqi), Allah makes ease for him in what befalls him of hardship.

The word amr means affair and state. The intended meaning: He makes for him, from his difficult affair in his view, ease, by the indication of the making of ease for his affair.

The particle (min) is for the figurative beginning, meaning accompaniment and association.

Yusr (ease) is the absence of difficulty, that is, the absence of hardships and disliked things.

The purpose of this is to affirm the promise of ease in what is by nature difficult, to encourage husbands to obey what Allah has commanded the husband: maintenance during the waiting period, and returning [to the wife], and leaving his dwelling for her residence if it cannot accommodate both of them; and what He has commanded the woman: observing the full term of the waiting period, not leaving, and similar matters.

The reference in His saying (﴿That is the command of Allah﴾) is to the rulings mentioned earlier from the beginning of the sura. This clause is parenthetical between the two conjoined clauses.

The word amr in His saying (﴿the command of Allah﴾) means His judgment and what He has legislated for you, as He said: (﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52]).

His sending it down (inzaluhu) means its communication to people through the Messenger ﷺ. It is called sending down as a figure of speech, comparing the nobility of its meanings and words to an elevated thing, since what is noble is imagined as elevated. This is a frequent metaphor in the Qur'an. Thus in His saying (﴿anzalahu﴾) there is an implicit metaphor (isti'ara makniyya).

The statement is a metonymy (kinaya) for urging concern for its preservation, acting upon it, and inciting people to compete in knowledge of it, since Allah has shown care for people in sending down to them what contains their wellbeing.

The exhortation to act upon what Allah has commanded is repeated, with the promise of what is greater than provision, relief from distress, and the facilitation of difficulties in this world. That is the expiation of misdeeds and the abundance of rewards.

The sentence is conjoined to the parenthetical sentence, so it has the status of a parenthesis.

The promise was expressed in the form of a conditional sentence in order to affirm the dependence of the answer upon its condition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 65, verses 4–5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And for those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months, and likewise for those who have not menstruated.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with His saying (﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]), for the waiting period there (ʿiddah) refers to menstrual cycles (aqrāʾ). That implies that the woman in this waiting period is one who has menstrual cycles. Thus there remains the explanation of the waiting period of the woman who has passed the age of menstruation, or the one who has not reached the age of those who menstruate, namely the young girl. Both of them are truly described as having despaired of menstruation, that is, at that time.

The pause (waqf) is at His saying (﴿and likewise for those who have not menstruated﴾), meaning that they are coordinated with those who have despaired.

Yaʾs (despair) is the absence of hope. What is despaired of in the verse is known from the context, from His saying (﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]), that is, they have despaired of menstruation, whether that despair comes after it has occurred repeatedly or because it has not appeared, meaning it has not stopped due to illness or breastfeeding. The age for this varies according to the individual and the region, just as the age at which menstruation begins varies. The determination of this age has been disputed by number of years. It was said: sixty years; and it was said: fifty-five. Leaving it unspecified by years is better, and this is only an approximation of the time of despair.

The purpose of the verse is clear, and it particularizes (takhsīs) the generality of His saying (﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228]) in Surat al-Baqarah. Surat al-Ṭalāq was revealed after Surat al-Baqarah.

The implication of the condition in His saying (﴿if you are in doubt﴾) and what is connected to it has been obscured. Most of the exegetes (ahl al-tafsīr) took this condition as connected to the statement in which it occurs, and that it is not connected to His saying (﴿Do not turn them out of their houses﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]) at the beginning of this surah, contrary to an eccentric and far-fetched interpretation that scatters the unity of the speech. Then the meaning of this condition was obscured by His saying (﴿if you are in doubt﴾).

Scholars have two approaches to this. The first approach: its proponents held that the referent of despair is not the referent of doubt, because the object of each differs. Ashhab related from Malik that when God, exalted is He, explained the waiting period of women who have menstrual cycles and women who are pregnant, that is, in Surat al-Baqarah, the despairing women and those who had not menstruated remained, and the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ were in doubt about their matter, so this verse was revealed. A similar report is transmitted from Mujahid. Al-Ṭabarī related a report: "From Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, that he asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the waiting period of these two, who were not mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, and this verse was revealed." They took the particle (in) to mean (idh) (when), and that the doubt occurred regarding the ruling on the waiting period before the revelation of the verse, that is: when you were in doubt about the ruling on that, we explained it by this verse. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "The hadith of Ubayy is not authentic." I say: It was related by al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan, and al-Ḥākim in al-Mustadrak, and he authenticated it. And al-Ṭabarānī with its chain from ʿAmr ibn Sālim, that Ubayy said. There is nothing in al-Ṭabarī's narration that indicates the chain of the hadith.

It is in al-Bayhaqī's narration with its chain to Abū ʿUthmān ʿUmar ibn Sālim al-Anṣārī, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and it is discontinuous (munqaṭiʿ), because Abū ʿUthmān did not meet Ubayy ibn Kaʿb. I suppose that it is also so in al-Ḥākim's Mustadrak, because al-Bayhaqī narrated it from al-Ḥākim. So there is no basis for Ibn al-ʿArabī's statement that it is not authentic, for the men in its chain are trustworthy (thiqāt).

In Asbāb al-Nuzūl of al-Wāḥidī, from Qatādah: "That Khallād ibn al-Nuʿmān and Ubayy asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about that, and this verse was revealed." It was said that the questioner was Muʿādh ibn Jabal, who asked about the waiting period of the woman who has despaired.

So the doubt on this approach means the uncertainty that arose regarding the ruling on these divorced women. Thus the conditional clause is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍ) between the subject, which is the relative pronoun, and its predicate, which is the clause (﴿their waiting period is three months﴾).

The fāʾ in (﴿fa-ʿiddatuhunna﴾) is attached to the predicate clause because the relative pronoun carries the meaning of a condition, like His saying (﴿And those two of you who commit it, harm them﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 16]), and similar examples are numerous in speech.

Doubt on this approach has already occurred in the past, so (in) is used in the sense of certainty without any special purpose.

The second approach: its proponents held that the referent of despair and the referent of doubt are one and the same, namely the state of the divorced woman with regard to menstruation. This is from ʿIkrimah, Qatādah and Ibn Zayd, and Yaḥyā ibn Bukayr and Ismāʿīl ibn Hād of the Mālikīs interpreted it this way, and Ibn Lubābah of the Mālikīs attributed it to Dāwūd al-Ẓāhirī.

This interpretation makes it clear that the meaning of doubt is the occurrence of uncertainty regarding the woman's condition.

On this basis, the conditional clause and its response is a statement about (﴿those who have despaired﴾), that is: if they (the women) are in doubt, and you (men) are in doubt because of their doubt. The masculine plural pronoun of addressees is then used with precedence (taghlīb), and the condition remains a condition. Doubt here is in the future, and the fāʾ is the linking particle of the response.

This interpretation implies that the waiting of three months is conditional on the occurrence of doubt about their despair of menstruation. Hence its proponents collided with the concept of the condition (mafhūm al-sharṭ), which implies that if doubt does not occur about their despair, they do not observe that waiting period, or they do not observe any waiting period at all. Ibn Lubābah, one of the Mālikī jurists, attributed to Dāwūd al-Ẓāhirī that he held the waiting period falls away for the woman whose despair is certain.

I say: this attribution to Dāwūd is not known. Ibn Ḥazm did not report it from him, nor did anyone who addressed the differences of the jurists report it. Ibn Lubābah said: "This is an anomaly (shudhūdh)." Ibn Lubābah also said: "As for Ibn Bukayr and Ismāʿīl ibn Ḥammād," that is, of the Mālikī jurists, "they made the woman whose despair is certain analogous to the doubtful woman in the waiting period by way of analogy (qiyās)," meaning that the waiting period has two wisdoms: the clearing of the womb, and the waiting for reconciliation. As for those who do not regard the concept of opposition (mafhūm al-mukhālafa), they are free of what binds those who regard it.

The proponents of this approach differ in the direction and in how the verse is to be understood accordingly. ʿIkrimah, Ibn Zayd and Qatādah said: the woman who is in doubt about the return of menstruation to her has no waiting period longer than three months, clinging to the apparent meaning of the verse. Probably the reason for this view is that within three months the matter of pregnancy becomes clear; if no pregnancy appears after it ends, the woman's waiting period is complete, because pregnancy after the age of despair is rare. But if doubt about pregnancy arises, the question shifts to the ruling on doubt about pregnancy, and that is a different issue from the one the verse was revealed about.

Most scholars said: the doubtful woman in her despair remains for nine months (that is, the usual period of pregnancy). If no pregnancy appears in her, she begins the waiting period of three months, so that she completes a full year. The basis of this is what Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab related from the judgment of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, and no one among the Companions disagreed, and Mālik adopted it. And from Mālik in al-Mudawwana: nine months for doubt, and the three months are the waiting period. Probably they regarded the waiting period after the passing of the nine months as a devotional matter (taʿabbud), because that is what is in the Qur'an. As for the nine months, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb made them obligatory, probably by ijtihād (independent reasoning), and it is a restriction (taqyīd) of the unrestricted generality found in the verse.

Al-Nakhaʿī, Sufyān al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī said: the doubtful woman in her despair observes the waiting period by menstrual cycles, that is, she waits for blood until she reaches the age of one who is not likely to menstruate, even if the period of her waiting exceeds nine months. When she reaches the age of despair without doubt, she observes a waiting period of three months from that day. We interpret their view by holding that the sense of the speech is: "their waiting period is three months," that is, after the cessation of doubt, as we shall mention. Yet this still implies that these three months after the passing of nine months, or after the passing of a period that brings her to the age of one who is not likely to menstruate, is a devotional matter, because the absence of pregnancy has become clear and the waiting for reconciliation has been prolonged. Unless we excuse them by saying that during the waiting period the divorcer is not yet moved to decide about reconciliation, since he is within the scope of waiting, and so the period is extended for that reason. In the tafsir of al-Qurṭubī: ʿIkrimah and Qatādah said: "Among the doubtful is the woman who has irregular bleeding, whose menstruation does not follow a regular pattern, sometimes at the beginning of the month, several times, and sometimes once in months," that is, without regularity. Al-Ṭabarī related similar words from al-Zuhrī and Ibn Zayd. So this aspect must be adopted in interpreting the verse. When a woman approaches the time of despair, menstruation does not cease from her all at once, but she remains for months with menstruation coming at intervals without regularity, until it ends entirely.

His saying (﴿and likewise for those who have not menstruated﴾) is coordinated with (﴿and those who have despaired﴾), and the implied sense is: "their waiting period is three months." It is good to pause at His saying (﴿their waiting period is three months﴾).

* * *

﴿And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they deliver their burden.﴾

It is coordinated with the clause (﴿and likewise for those who have not menstruated﴾). It completes the states of the waiting period, which were stated in summary in His saying (﴿and count the waiting period﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]). The implied sense is: (﴿and for those pregnant among them﴾), that is, among the divorced women, their term is until they deliver their burden.

Thus through this verse together with the preceding one, the states of the divorced women are detailed, and an explanation is also given of the summary in the verse in Surat al-Baqarah.

(﴿Ulāt﴾) is a plural noun meaning: those possessing. (Dhāt) is the feminine of (dhū), meaning: possessor. There is no singular of (ulāt) from its own form, just as there is no singular of the word (ulū), and (ulāt) is like (dhawāt), just as (ulū) is like (dhawū). (Ulāt) is written in the orthography with a waw after the hamza, following the spelling of the word (ulū) with a waw after the hamza, in order to distinguish in writing between (ulī) in the accusative and genitive cases and the preposition (ilā). I wish they had restricted this spelling with a waw after the hamza to the word (ulī) in the masculine accusative or genitive, and left aside the artificial spelling in other cases.

The waiting period of a divorced pregnant woman is ended by the delivery of the child, because nothing more clearly indicates the clearing of the womb, since the primary purpose of the waiting period is to establish the clearing of the womb of a child of the divorcer, or to make evident that the womb is occupied with a fetus of his. Another purpose was added to this, namely to await the regret of the divorcer and to enable him to correct his matter by reconciliation. When the more important purpose was achieved, the rest were set aside, in consideration of the woman's right to be freed from the hardship of waiting. Moreover, pregnancy may occur close to the time of divorce, so the purpose of waiting was set aside, with the reasoning based on what is usual rather than what is rare. This is in contrast to those who said regarding the widow: "She must observe the longer of the two terms," which is attributed to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and Ibn ʿAbbās.

With this interpretation, this verse does not conflict with the verse on the waiting period of the widow in Surat al-Baqarah (﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234]), because that is in one valley and this is in another. That is about widows, and this is about divorced women.

However, since the term of four months and ten days for the widow has a wisdom limited to ensuring the clearing of the womb of the deceased husband's wife from a child of his, for there is no benefit in it other than that, and it should not be imagined that the Sharīʿah prescribed it for the purpose of grieving for the deceased husband, since it is definitively established that this is a pre-Islamic aim, and the Sharīʿah in many places has nullified it and forbidden it in many forms, as we have explained in the commentary on His saying (﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234]) etc. in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 65, verses 4–5 (part 2 of 2):

We have already known that the delivery of the child is the terminal point for the achievement of this purpose. It follows from the meaning that a pregnant widow, when she delivers her child, exits the waiting period of widowhood and does not need to complete four months and ten days, just as, if the duration of her pregnancy exceeded four months and ten days, she would not be confined to the four months and ten days, since there is no wisdom in that.

On account of this, the verse indicates that the waiting period of a pregnant woman is the delivery of her child, whether she is observing a waiting period due to divorce or a waiting period due to death.

On account of this, the majority of the scholars (ahl al-'ilm), from the Companions onward, said: the waiting period of a pregnant widow is like her waiting period due to divorce, namely the delivery of her child. However, their statements indicate that among them were those who, in a conflict between two general (ʿumūm) texts, held that the later of the two general texts abrogates the other general text, and this is the method of the earlier scholars (al-mutaqaddimīn).

The people of the authentic collections (ahl al-Ṣaḥīḥ) narrated that 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, when it reached him that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib had said concerning the waiting period of a pregnant widow that she must observe the longer of the two terms (i.e., the term of delivering the child and the term of four months and ten days), said: "The shorter sura of women (i.e., the sura of Divorce) was revealed after the longer one (i.e., after the longest of the suras), which is al-Baqara." That is, the verse of al-Baqara does not abrogate what is in the verse of the sura of Divorce.

(And there supports them the report of Subay'a bint al-Harith al-Aslamiyya, whose husband Sa'd ibn Khawla died during the Farewell Pilgrimage in Makka and left her pregnant; she delivered [her child] fifteen nights after his death, and it was said forty nights. She asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for permission to remarry, and he said to her: "You have become free [of the waiting period]; marry if you wish." Umm Salama, the Mother of the Believers, narrated it, and most of the Companions who came to know of it accepted it. The jurists after them received it with acceptance, and it is witnessed to by its meaning and wisdom, as has been mentioned just above.)

The later scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (ahl al-Usul) differed regarding the manner of acting in a conflict between two general texts, each of which is general in one respect, like these two verses. The majority adopted the preference of one of them by means of a preponderating factor, while the Hanafis held that the later of the two general texts abrogates the earlier one. So His saying (﴿And those who are pregnant [have as their term] until they deliver their burdens﴾) — because the relative pronoun is among the forms of generality, it encompasses every pregnant woman observing a waiting period, whether it is a waiting period due to divorce or a waiting period due to death. And His saying (﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind—they [the wives] shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]) encompasses every woman whom the deceased left behind, whether pregnant or not pregnant, because (﴿wives﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]) is an indefinite noun that occurs as the object of the relative clause, and (﴿they leave behind﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]), which contains the pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun which is general, so its object follows it in its generality, and thus it includes the widows who are pregnant, who are among those encompassed by the generality of (﴿And those who are pregnant﴾). Thus the two generalities conflict, each in one respect. The verse (﴿And those who are pregnant﴾) requires that all pregnant women's waiting period ends with delivery, and it may be that delivery occurs before the four months and ten days; while the verse of al-Baqara, by its generality, requires that widows wait four months and ten days, and this term may extend beyond the delivery of the child.

The majority went to preferring the generality of (﴿And those who are pregnant﴾) over the generality of (﴿and leave wives behind﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]) for several reasons.

The first: the generality of (﴿And those who are pregnant﴾) arises from the very wording itself, because the relative pronoun together with its clause is among the forms of generality. As for His saying (﴿and leave wives behind﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]), (﴿wives﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]) is an indefinite noun in an affirmative context, so it has no generality in its own wording; generality came to it only incidentally, following the generality of the governing relative pronoun. That which is general by its essence is stronger than that which is general by accident.

The second: the ruling in the generality of (﴿And those who are pregnant﴾) is attached to the meaning of the relative clause, which is a derivative, and attaching a ruling to a derivative indicates the causal basis of that from which it is derived. Unlike the generality in the sura of al-Baqara, the generality whose ruling is causally linked to an attribute is stronger in application than the generality whose ruling is not causally linked.

The third: the judgment of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning the waiting period of Subay'a al-Aslamiyya.

The Hanafis went to the view that the generality of (﴿And those who are pregnant﴾) abrogates the generality of His saying (﴿and leave wives behind﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]) to the extent to which the two conflicted.

The outcome of the two opinions is one: the waiting period of a pregnant woman is the delivery of her child, whether she is observing a waiting period due to divorce or due to the death of her husband.

The correct view is that the ruling of the verse of al-Baqara has not been lifted, and those who held that a widow who is not pregnant, if she delivers her child, must still observe a waiting period of four months and ten days are anomalous.

A few scholars held that the two verses should be reconciled in a way that realises the implementation of both together. They obligated the pregnant widow to observe the longer of the two terms: the term of four months and ten days and the term of delivering the child. This is the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas. Their aim in this is precaution, since the conflict here concerns the measure of two periods of time, so it was possible to act upon the wider of the two, which contains the other and something more. The meaning of this verse thus becomes: (﴿And those who are pregnant—their term is that they deliver their burden﴾) provided they are not in a waiting period due to death; and the meaning of the verse of al-Baqara becomes: and those widows whose husbands have died shall wait by themselves four months and ten days, provided they are not pregnant, for if they are pregnant they extend their waiting until delivery. And the generality of (﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind—they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]) is not to be specified by what is in the verse (﴿And those who are pregnant—their term is that they deliver their burden﴾) regarding the specificity concerning pregnant widows, since it is not permissible for the waiting period of a pregnant widow who has passed four months and ten days to end before she delivers her child, while she is still pregnant, because the invalidity of this is established by several proofs in the Sharia about which there is no disagreement. This is also the view of Ibn Abi Layla.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: "I was in a circle of notable Ansar" — that is, in Kufa — "and among them was 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, and his companions were admonishing him. He mentioned the later of the two terms, so I narrated the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba concerning the case of Subay'a bint al-Harith. 'Abd al-Rahman said: 'But his paternal uncle' — that is, the paternal uncle of 'Utba, who is 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud — 'did not used to say that' — that is, he did not narrate it to us. So I said: 'Then I would indeed be bold if I lied about a man on the outskirts of Kufa.' 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba was residing on the outskirts of Kufa. So I went out and met 'Amir or Malik ibn 'Awf, and I said: 'What was the statement of Ibn Mas'ud concerning a widow who is pregnant?' He said: 'Ibn Mas'ud said: "Do you impose the strictness upon her and not grant her the concession? The shorter sura of women was revealed after the longer one" (i.e., al-Baqara).'"

In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Abu Salama: a man came to Ibn 'Abbas while Abu Hurayra was sitting with him, and said: "Give me a ruling concerning a woman who gave birth forty nights after her husband." Ibn 'Abbas said: "The later of the two terms." I said: "(﴿And those who are pregnant—their term is that they deliver their burden﴾)." Abu Hurayra said: "I am with my nephew" — that is, with Abu Salama. Then Ibn 'Abbas sent Kurayb to Umm Salama to ask her, and she said: "He was killed" — (so it is said, though the verification is that he died during the Farewell Pilgrimage) — "the husband of Subay'a al-Aslamiyya, while she was pregnant, and she delivered forty nights after his death; then she was proposed to, and the Messenger of Allah married her off." Some have said that Ibn 'Abbas retracted his statement, but his retraction is not mentioned in the hadith of Abu Salama.

* * *

(﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him ease in his affair﴾) (﴿That is the command of Allah, which He has sent down to you; and whoever fears Allah, He will remove from him his misdeeds and enlarge for him a reward﴾).

This is a repetition of the admonition, and it is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad). What is said about it is the same as what is said about His saying, exalted is He (﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2] (﴿and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 3])). The purpose is to admonish men and women to adhere to what is in these rulings, which may involve hardship for someone, by way of obligating each to be patient in that in obedience to the command of Allah, for the one who complies, who is named the God-fearing (al-muttaqi), Allah makes ease for him in what befalls him of hardship.

The word amr means affair and state. The intended meaning: He makes for him, from his difficult affair in his view, ease, by the indication of the making of ease for his affair.

The particle (min) is for the figurative beginning, meaning accompaniment and association.

Yusr (ease) is the absence of difficulty, that is, the absence of hardships and disliked things.

The purpose of this is to affirm the promise of ease in what is by nature difficult, to encourage husbands to obey what Allah has commanded the husband: maintenance during the waiting period, and returning [to the wife], and leaving his dwelling for her residence if it cannot accommodate both of them; and what He has commanded the woman: observing the full term of the waiting period, not leaving, and similar matters.

The reference in His saying (﴿That is the command of Allah﴾) is to the rulings mentioned earlier from the beginning of the sura. This clause is parenthetical between the two conjoined clauses.

The word amr in His saying (﴿the command of Allah﴾) means His judgment and what He has legislated for you, as He said: (﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52]).

His sending it down (inzaluhu) means its communication to people through the Messenger ﷺ. It is called sending down as a figure of speech, comparing the nobility of its meanings and words to an elevated thing, since what is noble is imagined as elevated. This is a frequent metaphor in the Qur'an. Thus in His saying (﴿anzalahu﴾) there is an implicit metaphor (isti'ara makniyya).

The statement is a metonymy (kinaya) for urging concern for its preservation, acting upon it, and inciting people to compete in knowledge of it, since Allah has shown care for people in sending down to them what contains their wellbeing.

The exhortation to act upon what Allah has commanded is repeated, with the promise of what is greater than provision, relief from distress, and the facilitation of difficulties in this world. That is the expiation of misdeeds and the abundance of rewards.

The sentence is conjoined to the parenthetical sentence, so it has the status of a parenthesis.

The promise was expressed in the form of a conditional sentence in order to affirm the dependence of the answer upon its condition.

**[Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr, *al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr*, on Sūrat al-Ṭalāq, verse 6]**

﴿Lodge them where you dwell, according to your means.﴾

This sentence and the sentences attached to it, up to His words (﴿And how many a city rebelled﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 8]), etc.

This is a new legislative section (*tashrīʿ mustaʾnaf*) that explains what was stated in general terms in the preceding verses: His words (﴿Do not expel them from their homes﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]), His words (﴿or part from them with kindness﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 2]), and His words (﴿And for those with children, their term is until they give birth﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 4]). These sentences, in relation to the ones before them, take the position of an explanation of some parts by others. Their connection is one of inclusion (*ishtimāl*), and all of this requires a separation (*fasl*). It begins with explaining what was general in (﴿Do not expel them from their homes﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]).

The object pronoun in (﴿Lodge them﴾) refers to the divorced women mentioned in His words (﴿When you divorce women﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]). Nothing in what precedes can be the referent of this pronoun except the word "women" and the phrase (﴿those with children﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 4]). However, no one has said that lodging is specific to pregnant women in their waiting period, because that would contradict His words (﴿Do not expel them﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]). Therefore the pronoun must refer to all divorced women, and so it includes the revocably divorced woman (*al-muṭallaqa al-rajʿiyya*), the irrevocably divorced woman (*al-bāʾina*), and the pregnant woman, in accordance with what you know from the beginning of the sūra about the meaning of the phrase (﴿When you divorce women﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]) as including both revocable and irrevocable divorce.

The majority of scholars hold that lodging is obligatory for all of them. Ashhab said: Mālik said, "He leaves the dwelling when he divorces her, and she remains in the house." Ibn Nāfiʿ reported that Mālik said: "As for the woman who has not become irrevocably separated, she is a wife, and they inherit from each other, and lodging is binding on their husbands for them." He means that she is exempt from deriving the ruling on her lodging from this verse, not that she is excluded from the ruling of the verse.

Qatāda, Ibn Abī Layla, Isḥāq, Abū Thawr and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: There is no lodging for a woman divorced with an irrevocable divorce (*ṭalāqan bāʾinan*). Their proof is what Fāṭima bint Qays narrated: that her husband divorced her three times, that his brother prevented her from lodging and maintenance, and that she brought her case to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said to her: "Lodging and maintenance are only for the one who has the right of return (*al-rajʿa*) over her." This is a rare report (*gharīb*) which no one knew except through Fāṭima bint Qays. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb did not accept it. He said: "We will not abandon the Book of God and the Sunna of our Prophet for the word of a woman; we do not know, perhaps she forgot or it was confused for her." ʿĀʾisha also denied Fāṭima bint Qays's report regarding his having permitted her to move to a place other than the one where she had been divorced, as mentioned earlier.

It is also reported that ʿUmar narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "the irrevocably divorced woman has lodging." They also narrated that Qatāda and Ibn Abī Layla took their position based on the words of God (﴿You do not know, perhaps God will bring about some matter after that﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]), since "the matter" is the return (*al-murājaʿa*). Thus they restricted the divorce in His words (﴿When you divorce women﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]) to revocable divorce, because after an irrevocable divorce no return is anticipated. Fāṭima bint Qays, mentioned above, had preceded them to this line of reasoning.

Muslim reported that Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam sent to Fāṭima bint Qays asking her about the report, and she narrated it to him. Marwān said: "We have only heard this report from a woman. We will adopt the established practice (*ʿiṣma*) that we found people following." When Marwān's words reached Fāṭima bint Qays, she said: "Between me and you is the Qur'an." God, Mighty and Majestic, said (﴿Do not expel them from their homes﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]) up to His words (﴿You do not know, perhaps God will bring about some matter after that﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]). She said: "This applies to the one who has a right of return. What matter could arise after three divorces?"

This is refuted by the fact that the bringing about of a matter is not confined to the return. Among the matters God may bring about is softening their hearts so that both of them desire to resume marital life together through a new contract. Even if we concede that this is confined to the matter of return, mentioning this wisdom does not require restricting the generality of the wording before it, since it is sufficient that it be a wisdom for some situations of the general ruling. So the correct view is that the right to lodging belongs to all divorced women, which is the position of the majority of scholars.

His words (﴿from where you dwell﴾), i.e., in the houses you live in, mean that the divorcer is not required to provide a place for the divorced woman other than his own house, nor may he prevent her from lodging in his house. This is an emphasis of His words (﴿Do not expel them from their homes﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]).

If the dwelling cannot accommodate two separate households for overnight stay, the divorcing husband leaves it and the divorced woman remains, as was mentioned earlier in what Ashhab transmitted from Mālik.

The *min* in (﴿from where you dwell﴾) is partitive (*li-l-tabʿīḍ*), i.e., "from part of what you dwell in." From this it is understood that a dwelling may be partitioned according to the customary practice of lodging, while avoiding proximity in overnight stays if she is not revocably divorced. Thus it is understood that if the dwelling cannot accommodate both of them, the divorcing husband leaves.

The *min* in His words (﴿according to your means﴾) is a congruent apposition (*badal muṭābiq*), and it explains His words (﴿from where you dwell﴾), since a man's dwelling is ordinarily the means he has found, for one who is not stingy with himself.

The word *wujd* (with the vowel on the *wāw* variable, all three vowels being permitted) means capacity and ability. The majority read it with a *ḍamma* on the *wāw*. Rawḥ, from Yaʿqūb, read it with a *kasra*.

* * *

﴿And do not harm them in order to constrain them.﴾

After the command to lodge the divorced women, a prohibition against harming them in any way during the waiting period is attached: whether by narrowing the place, by stinginess in spending, or by a return followed by divorce again in order to prolong their waiting period, with the intention of vexing and gloating over them, as was explained earlier at His words (﴿And do not take the signs of God in jest﴾ [al-Baqara: 231]) in Sūrat al-Baqara. Or it may be to compel her to ransom herself from his return through *khulʿ* (divorce for compensation).

*al-ḍārr* is strong harm, so the intensification (*mubālagha*) returns to the prohibition, not to the thing prohibited. That is, it is a strong prohibition, like the intensification in His words (﴿And your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 46]), in that it is an intensification of negation. Similar examples are numerous in the Qur'an.

By *taḍyīq* (constraining) is meant figurative constraint, which is hardship and harm.

The *lām* in (﴿in order to constrain them﴾) indicates the cause of the harm. This is a qualifier that follows the most common of the intentions of the people of ignorance (*ahl al-jāhiliyya*) toward divorced people, as was established in His words (﴿And do not keep them to harm them so that you transgress﴾ [al-Baqara: 231]). Otherwise, harming divorced women is prohibited even if it is not intended to constrain them.

* * *

﴿And if they are pregnant, spend on them until they give birth.﴾

The pronoun in (*kunna*) refers to what the pronoun in (﴿lodge them﴾) referred to, as is the norm in the arrangement of pronouns and as is required by the coordination of sentences. It does not refer specifically to the women who are lodged, because a pronoun cannot be the referent of another pronoun.

The apparent structure of the verse suggests that pregnant women are entitled to maintenance, not some of the divorced women, by taking the implication of the condition (*mafhūm al-sharṭ*). Al-Shāfiʿī, al-Awzāʿī and Ibn Abī Layla took this view.

However, this implication is inoperative for revocably divorced women, because their maintenance is established by the fact that they are wives. For this reason Mālik said that the pronoun in (﴿lodge them﴾) refers to irrevocably divorced women, as mentioned above. Those who do not adopt the implication say that the verse addresses pregnant women to emphasize maintenance for them, because the period of pregnancy is long and the divorcer might grow weary of spending. Thus the purpose of this sentence is the limit expressed by (﴿until they give birth﴾). They made maintenance due to a divorced woman who is not pregnant. Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Thawrī also took this view, and it is attributed to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with them both.

What favors this view is that a condition has no implication here; rather the condition is brought in to encompass the entire duration of the pregnancy in maintenance.

* * *

﴿And if they nurse for you, give them their wages, and confer among yourselves in kindness. But if you disagree, then another woman will nurse for him.﴾

When pregnancy ends with delivery, the discussion moves on to what is due to them after delivery. By giving birth they become irrevocably separated, and the rules of marriage are cut off. So the hearer may not know whether her nursing her child is a duty upon her as it was during the marital bond, or a duty upon her husband, so that he gives her the wage for nursing just as he used to give her maintenance for that child while it was in the womb. This verse specifies the words of God in *Sūrat al-Baqara* (﴿And mothers nurse their children﴾ [al-Baqara: 233]) and what follows.

His words (*lakum*, "for you") imply that nursing the child after separation is a duty upon the father alone, because it is like maintenance. According to Mālik the mother nurses her child during the marriage as a consequence of her husband's maintenance of her. This differs from Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī, who say: nursing is not obligatory upon the mother even during the marriage. Once the father's maintenance of her ceases with the irrevocable separation, the sustenance of his son becomes entirely his responsibility. If she wishes to nurse him, she has the better claim to that and she has the wage for nursing. If she refuses, then he must seek a wet-nurse (*ẓi'r*) for his son. If the infant refuses the breast of anyone other than his mother, nursing becomes obligatory upon her, and it becomes obligatory upon his father to pay the wage for his nursing.

Abū Thawr said: nursing the son is obligatory upon his mother even after the irrevocable separation. Ibn al-ʿArabī reported this from him in *al-Aḥkām*, and it is strange, since this verse is before him.

*al-ʾitimār* means consultation and deliberation over an opinion. Its root is the reflexive form of *amara* (to command), because two people consulting each other command one another, and the other complies with what he is commanded. From this comes the naming of gatherings of the people of a call, a sect, or a unified aim as a *muʾtamar* (conference), because consultation (*istiʾmār*) takes place there, that is, deliberation and exchange of opinions.

His words (﴿and confer among yourselves﴾) address men and women among whom divorce has occurred, so that they may consult about the matter of the mother nursing her child and what the father pays her for that.

The consultation is qualified by "in kindness" (*bi-maʿrūf*), meaning a consultation consistent with what is customary for people in their situation and their community, that is, customary and acceptable. So the father should not be miserly, nor should the mother be excessively greedy.

His words (﴿But if you disagree, then another woman will nurse for him﴾) are a rebuke and an admonition to both the father and the mother, so that each of them places himself or herself in the position of someone to whom a wet-nurse would be brought for the infant. Thus the mother should not demand more than the wage of women like her, and the father should not be stingy with what reaches the wage of the child's mother. Nor does the mother's right lapse if the father finds someone who will nurse for him for free, because God said (﴿then another woman will nurse for him﴾), and one says "she nursed for him" only when she was hired for that purpose, just as one says "he hired a nurse" (*istarḍaʿa*) when he hires someone to nurse his child. His words (﴿And if you wish to have your children nursed by another woman﴾ [al-Baqara: 233]) and what follows were mentioned earlier in *Sūrat al-Baqara*.

*al-taʿāsur* is the occurrence of hardship from both sides. It is a reciprocal form (*tafāʿul*) derived from your saying "ʿasarta fulānan," meaning when you took someone in his hardship. One says "the two sellers disagreed" (*taʿāsara*) when they did not agree.

So the meaning of (﴿you disagree﴾) is that disagreement between you has intensified and you have not returned to agreement, so the child should not be left without nursing.

The *sīn* of the future (*sīn al-istiqbāl*) is used to express emphasis, as in His words (﴿He said: I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ [Yūsuf: 98]) in *Sūrat Yūsuf*. This meaning arises from making the sign of the future a metonymy (*kināya*) for the renewal of that action in future times, in order to affirm its occurrence.

This statement is also used metonymically to express the father's command to hire a wet-nurse for the infant, by the indication of the phrase *lahu* ("for him") being linked to (﴿will nurse﴾).

Thus three metonymies are combined in it: a metonymy for the admonition of the father, a metonymy for the admonition of the mother, and a metonymy for the father's command to have his child nursed.
