**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 65, verse 7:**

﴿Let the one of wealth spend from his wealth, and whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend from what Allah has given him. Allah does not burden a soul except with what He has given it. Allah will bring about, after hardship, ease.﴾

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) following the rulings on spending that were mentioned earlier concerning women in waiting period and nursing mothers, encompassing all of that. It also encompasses every kind of spending the Muslim is required to make, whether obligatory or recommended, meaning spending in proportion to one's means.

Al-sa'ah (means/abundance) is the newness or sufficiency of wealth or provision.

Al-infaq (spending) is providing for the necessities of life: food, clothing, and other things needed.

Here "min" (from) is for beginning (ibtida'iyyah), because spending proceeds from one's means in consideration. It is not like the "min" in His saying, ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], because spending here is not a part of one's means, whereas there it is a part of provision. Therefore the "min" in ﴿let him spend from what Allah has given him﴾ is partitive (tab'idiyyah).

The meaning of ﴿his provision has been restricted﴾ is that his provision has been made limited, bounded by a specific measure, and this is a metaphor for constriction. Its opposite is ﴿they will be provided for therein without account﴾ [Ghafir: 40]. One says "qudira 'alayhi rizquhu" when he restricts it, as He said, ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26], which has been discussed in Surah al-Ra'd. That is: whoever is in narrowness of wealth, let him spend in what his provision permits, considering fulfilment of spending and its degrees of priority. This is stated briefly here, and its details are in other evidences from the Book, the Sunnah, and deduction. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Hind bint 'Utbah, wife of Abu Sufyan: "Take from his wealth what suffices you and your child, in a reasonable manner."

Al-ma'ruf is what people have customarily accepted in their usual dealings, as long as the Sharia has not nullified it.

Al-rizq is a name for what a person benefits from in his needs: food, clothing, goods, and housing, whether they are commodities or currency. The word rizq is often applied to food, as in His saying, ﴿he found with her provision﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 37].

The scholars do not differ that maintenance is not fixed by specific amounts, because the circumstances of people, times, and lands differ. They differed only about whether the wealthy man's expenditure is to be extended to those he supports, and I do not think the disagreement on this is other than a disagreement about people's conditions and customs. It is necessary to consider the condition of the one who is supported and his customary standard, such as a wife of high rank. All of this falls under the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Hind: "what suffices you and your child, in a reasonable manner."

The clause ﴿Allah does not burden a soul except with what He has given it﴾ gives the reason for His saying ﴿whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend from what Allah has given him﴾, because the content of this clause was already established among the Muslims earlier in His saying ﴿Allah does not burden a soul except with its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286] in Surah al-Baqarah, which comes before Surah al-Talaq.

Its purpose is to persuade the one being supported that he should not ask the spender for more than his capacity. For this reason our scholars said: one is not called "poor" (mu'sir) if he is able to feed and clothe the one he supports in a reasonable manner, even if with hardship, meaning without harm.

The phrase ﴿from what Allah has given him﴾ includes the capacity to earn. So if one who is obligated to spend is able to earn, in order that he may spend on those whose maintenance is incumbent upon him, or to complete what his wealth falls short of, he is compelled to earn. As for one who has no capacity to earn and has nothing to spend from, his maintenance, or the maintenance of those whose support is incumbent upon him, in its various degrees, is upon the public treasury of the Muslims. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Indeed the owner of the small flock and the owner of the little herd, if their livestock perish, they will come with evidence saying: O Commander of the Believers, O Commander of the Believers. Shall I abandon them?" Malik narrated it in the Muwatta'.

Regarding the husband's inability to maintain his wife when she seeks separation due to lack of maintenance, there is disagreement. Some jurists held that this requires separation between them after a waiting period of hope that pleases the husband, estimated at two months, and this is the view of Malik. Others did not see separation between the spouses on this basis, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah, meaning that she is maintained from the public treasury of the Muslims.

What the analysis requires is that if the public treasury exists, it is incumbent upon it to maintain the needy spouses. If the maintenance cannot be obtained from the public treasury, it is right that the judge separate them and not leave the woman and her husband in need. The detailed discussion of this belongs in the books of jurisprudence.

The clause ﴿Allah will bring about, after hardship, ease﴾ completes the concluding statement, for His saying ﴿Allah does not burden a soul except with what He has given it﴾ corresponds to the content of the clause ﴿let the one of wealth spend from his wealth﴾.

And His saying ﴿Allah will bring about﴾ etc. corresponds to the content of ﴿whoever has his provision restricted﴾ etc. This statement is a report used to arouse hope and remove despair from the needy one among those with dependents. Its meaning: perhaps Allah will bring about ease for you after your hardship, for Allah brings about ease after hardship. This report only requires that it is among Allah's dealings to bring about ease for a people after their hardship, so whoever is in hardship hopes to be among those encompassed by Allah's bounty, and He will replace his hardship with ease.

There is no promise in this report to every needy person that his hardship will become ease. Observation may contradict this, and there is no benefit in forcing the claim that this is a promise from Allah to the Muslim believers of that time that Allah would replace their hardship with ease, or a promise to the spenders who obey Allah's command and do not withhold anything of what their wealth allows. Consider His saying, ﴿Indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾ [al-Sharh: 5].

Among the eloquence of the Qur'an is the use of "'usr" and "yusr" as indefinite nouns, without the definite article, lest definiteness be taken to mean totality (istighraq), as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾ [al-Sharh: 5].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 65, verses 8–9:

﴿And how many a town rebelled against the command of its Lord and His messengers, so We called it to a severe reckoning and punished it with a terrible punishment.﴾ ﴿So it tasted the evil consequence of its affair, and the outcome of its affair was loss.﴾ ﴿Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment.﴾ [al-Talaq: 10].

When many rulings concerning divorce and its related matters were legislated for the Muslims, and all of them were obligations that some souls might shrink from fulfilling fully, out of laziness or negligence, He encouraged compliance with them through His saying (﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]), His saying (﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him ease in his affair﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]), His saying (﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will remove from him his misdeeds and enlarge for him his reward﴾ [al-Talaq: 5]), and His saying (﴿Allah will bring about, after hardship, ease﴾ [al-Talaq: 7]).

In the course of this, Allah warned people against violating them through His saying (﴿These are the limits of Allah, and whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has certainly wronged himself﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]) and His saying (﴿This is admonished to whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]). He followed this with a great warning against falling into opposition to the rulings of Allah and His messengers, because of the scant care given to observing them, for the small leads to the great (al-sagheer yuthiru al-jaleel). So He reminded the Muslims, who are not among those who rebel against the command of their Lord, of the great punishment that befell peoples for their scant regard for the command of Allah and His messengers, lest they follow the path of negligence in establishing the Shari'ah, for that would throw them into the abyss of error.

This discourse is an introduction to what follows in His saying (﴿So fear Allah, O people of understanding﴾ [al-Talaq: 10]) and the verses after it. The sentence is therefore conjoined (ma'tuf) to the whole group of preceding sentences, as a conjunction of one purpose upon another purpose.

*Ka'ayyin* (كَأيِّنْ) is a noun denoting a large, indefinite number, which is specified by the noun in the genitive governed by *min* that follows it. *Ka'ayyin* has the meaning of the interrogative-informative *kam* (how many). It was discussed earlier at His saying (﴿And how many a prophet fought, and with him were many devoted men﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 146]) in Surah Ali 'Imran.

The purpose of expressing multiplicity here is to establish that the punishment that befell the people of those towns was something inherent in their recompense for their rebellion against the command of their Lord and His messengers. Thus no one should imagine that it was a coincidence affecting some towns only, and that it was not consistent across all of them.

*Ka'ayyin* is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), and it is indeclinable (mabni). The sentence (﴿'ataat 'an amri rabbiha﴾, "they rebelled against the command of their Lord") is in the position of the predicate of *ka'ayyin*.

The meaning is the report of the abundance of that, in terms of what is derived from it in His saying (﴿so We called it to account﴾). The derived element is thus the intended aim of the predicate.

By "town" (al-qarya) is meant its people, in the manner of His saying (﴿And ask the town in which we were﴾ [Yusuf: 82]), as indicated by His saying immediately after (﴿Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment﴾ [al-Talaq: 10]), where a pronoun for a plural of rational beings is used.

The word "town" was chosen here rather than "nation" or similar because the use of this term carries an allusion to the polytheists of Makkah, and an accompaniment of them in warning. For this reason, the mention of the people of towns is frequent in the Qur'an when reminding of Allah's punishment, as in His saying (﴿And how many a town We destroyed﴾ [al-A'raf: 4]).

Within it is a reminder to the Muslims of Allah's promise of their victory and the annihilation of their enemy.

*Al-'utuww* (العُتُوُّ), also said *al-'utiyy* (العُتِيُّ), means exceeding the limit in arrogance and obstinacy. It was implicitly given the sense of turning away, and so it takes the preposition *'an* (عَنْ).

*Al-muhasaba* (المُحاسَبَة) here is used for recompense for the deed, with a punishment proportionate to its severity, likening the determination of recompense to the settling of accounts between dealing parties. This is the reckoning in this world. For this reason, (*hasabnaha*, "We called it to account") and (*'adhdhabnaha*, "We punished it") came in the past tense.

The meaning is: We repaid them for their rebellion with a recompense that matched their transgression.

*Al-'adhab al-nukur* (the terrible punishment) is the punishment of annihilation, by drowning, by being swallowed up by the earth, by stoning, and the like.

The conjunction of punishment to reckoning indicates that it is other than it. So the reckoning in what they encountered before annihilation consists of frightening warnings and signs of admonition, such as famine, plague, and punishment, which is what they were threatened with.

You may also take the reckoning literally, and mean by it the reckoning of the Hereafter. Its severity is the intensity of the scrutiny in it and the rebuke for every evil for which they are called to account.

[p. 335]

The punishment is the punishment of Hell. The past-tense verb is used with the meaning of the future, likening the future to the past in the certainty of its occurrence, as in His saying (﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]) and His saying (﴿And the companions of Paradise will call out to the companions of the Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 44]).

*Al-nukur* (النُّكُرُ) with two dammas, or with one damma and a sukun, is what reason denies because of the horror of its manner, a severe denial.

Nafi', Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read *nukuran* with two dammas. The rest read it with a sukun on the *kaf*. This was discussed in Surah al-Kahf.

The *fa'* in His saying (﴿So it tasted the evil consequence of its affair﴾) is for the sequence following (﴿So We called it to account﴾) and (﴿and We punished it﴾).

*Al-dhawq* (the tasting) here means sensing in general, and this is a metonymy of a general kind (majaz mursal).

*Al-wabil* (الوَبِيلُ) is an adjective of the form of a stable quality. It is said: *wabula* (وبُلَ), with a damma, of pasture, when its grass was unwholesome and harmful to what grazes on it.

*Al-amr* (الأمْرُ) means the condition and the state of affairs. The attribution of *al-wabal* to *al-amr* is an attribution of the effect to the cause: they tasted the evil consequence which their affair and state, in which they were, had caused for them.

*'Aqibat al-amr* (عاقِبَةُ الأمْرِ) means its end and its result. It covers the consequence in this world and the Hereafter, as indicated by His saying (﴿Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment﴾ [al-Talaq: 10]).

Their evil end is likened to the loss of a merchant in his trade, in that when they rebelled, they thought they had satisfied themselves by turning away from the messengers and prevailing over them, but before long they became humiliated, just as a merchant loses in his trade.

The verb *kana* (كانَ) is in the past form because the discussion concerns their consequence in this world, by way of dominance. In all of this there is an exaggerated portrayal of what befell them, emphasising the warning against what they fell into.

The sentence (﴿Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment﴾ [al-Talaq: 10]) is either a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the sentence (﴿and the outcome of its affair was loss﴾), or a partial substitute (badal ba'd min kull).

[p. 336]

The intended meaning is the punishment of the Hereafter, because *al-i'dad* (الإعْداد) means preparation, and only something that has not yet come about is prepared.

If you take the reckoning and the punishment mentioned just before as the reckoning and punishment of the Hereafter, as already stated, then the sentence (﴿Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment﴾ [al-Talaq: 10]) is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) explaining that this increases without being lessened, like His saying (﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾ [al-Naba': 30]).

He, may He be exalted, said (﴿Unquestionably, the allies of Allah – no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve﴾ [Yunus: 62] ﴿Those who believed and were fearing Allah﴾ [Yunus: 63]). His saying "ulu" means "dhu" (possessors of), and its explanation has already preceded at His saying (﴿And those who have despaired of menstruation﴾ [At-Talaq: 4]) just above. And (﴿those who have believed﴾) is a substitute (badal) for (ulu al-albab). This following indicates that their acceptance of faith is a sign of the soundness of their intellects. And the bringing of the relative clause is a notice that faith is a cause of piety and encompasses most of it, but piety has degrees, and those are what they were commanded to encompass.

* * *

﴿Allah has certainly sent down to you a reminder﴾ ﴿a messenger reciting to you the clear revelations of Allah, that he may bring those who believe and do righteous deeds out of darknesses into light﴾ [At-Talaq: 11].

In this sentence there is the meaning of cause for the command to piety, because the sending down of the Book is a great benefit to them, deserving their gratitude for it.

The emphasis of the report with (qad) is for attention to it and for arousing souls to peruse this Book and to follow the guidance of the Messenger (ﷺ).

The "reminder" (dhikr) is the Qur'an. It has been called dhikr in many verses because it contains reminding people of what they are heedless of, namely the proofs of monotheism and what branches from it of good conduct, then reminding them of the duties it contains, which we explained at His saying (﴿And they said, "O you to whom the reminder has been sent down"﴾ [Al-Hijr: 6]) in Surat al-Hijr. The sending down of the Qur'an is its conveyance to the Messenger (ﷺ) through the angel, and "sending down" is used for it as a metaphor, because the reminder is likened to a thing raised in the heavens, as preceded in Surat al-Hijr and in many verses.

The sending down of the reminder is attributed to the believers because they are the ones who benefited from it and knew what is in it; so they are singled out here from among all nations, though the Qur'an was sent down to all people.

His saying (﴿a messenger﴾ [At-Talaq: 11]) is a substitute (badal) for (dhikran), a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because between the Qur'an and the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) there is a close association and connection, for the messengerhood was realized for him at the descent of the Qur'an upon him. So the verb (anzala, "sent down") has been made to govern (ra'sulan) in accordance with its governing of the thing substituted, by reason of this concomitance and the inclusion of the concept of one of the two nouns within the concept of the other. This is like (﴿a messenger from Allah﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 2]) being substituted for His saying (﴿until there comes to them the clear evidence﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 1]) in Surat al-Bayyinah.

And the Messenger (rasul) is Muhammad (ﷺ).

As for interpreting the dhikr as Jibril, which is narrated from al-Kalbi in order to correct the substitution of (﴿rasulan﴾ [At-Talaq: 11]) from it, there are in it unnecessary strained interpretations, for there is no escape from considering the substitution of inclusion, and it is not correct to describe Jibril as one who recites the verses to people, since the meaning of recitation is far from that; likewise the interpretation of dhikr as Jibril.

It is also permissible that (﴿rasulan﴾ [At-Talaq: 11]) be an object of an omitted verb indicated by "Allah has sent down," and its estimate would be: "and He sent to you a messenger," and its omission would be for brevity; however, the former aspect is more eloquent and more concise.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (mubayyinatin) with a fatha on the ya'. The rest read it with a kasra, and the outcome of both readings is one.

The cause of the sending down of the reminder has been made the bringing out of the righteous believers from darknesses into light, although the cause of its sending down is the bringing out of all people from the darknesses of disbelief and corruption of deeds into the light of faith and righteous deeds; this is by consideration of the particular group who benefited from this reminder, out of concern for their affair. That does not indicate that the cause is restricted to this group, but it is merely a specification by mention. A parallel to this sentence has preceded in many places, among them the beginning of Surat al-A'raf.

This is a continuation of the command to be mindful of God (*taqwa*), and an honouring of the God-conscious (*muttaqun*) and a concern for them. This promise of everlasting bliss in exchange for their obedience is phrased as a conditional (*shart*) to indicate that this bliss is conditional upon its seekers believing and doing righteous deeds.

The word ﴿صالِحًا﴾ (*ṣāliḥan*) is an adjective (*naʿt*) of an omitted noun indicated by ﴿يَعْمَلْ﴾ (*yaʿmal*, "does") [al-Nisa': 110], meaning "a righteous deed." It is indefinite (*nakira*) in the context of a conditional, which conveys generality, just as it does in the context of negation. The meaning is: "and does all righteous deeds," meaning those that are commanded with a firm command, as indicated by the inductive study (*istiqra'*) of the evidences of the Sharia.

A parallel to this verse has occurred in many places in the Qur'an.

The clause ﴿قَدْ أحْسَنَ اللَّهُ لَهُ رِزْقًا﴾ ("God has indeed provided well for him with provision") is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in the accusative case in ("nudkhiluhu," "We will admit him"). Therefore, the mention of the Name of Majesty (God) here is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, so that the clause stands independently by itself.

*Al-rizq* (provision) is everything from which one benefits. Its indefiniteness here is for magnification, meaning "a great provision."

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿نُدْخِلْهُ﴾ (*nudkhiluhu*) with the *nun* of majesty (first person plural). The rest read it with the *ya'* (third person), referring it back to the Name of God in the phrase ﴿ومَن يُؤْمِن بِاللَّهِ﴾ ("whoever believes in God"). On the reading of Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, there is an *iltifat* (shift in grammatical person), in which the speech shifts from the third person to the first.

[p. 339]

*Allāh* (the Name of Majesty) is the predicate of an elided subject, its full form being: *huwa Allāh* ("He is God"). This is an instance of omitting the subject (*ḥadhf al-musnad ilayhi*) for the sake of established usage, as al-Sakkākī termed it. After the discourse had dealt with some of the greatest of God's affairs, beginning from His words ﴿And fear God, your Lord﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1] up to this point, the Name of Majesty, its pronoun, and the predications made of it had been repeated about thirty times. Therefore the context called for an increase in people's awareness of this Great One, and once the discourse had become full of mention of His Name, it was correct to omit it when predicating something of Him, for brevity. This was previously discussed at His words ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ [Maryam: 65] in Sūrat Maryam, and likewise at His words ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18] and His words ﴿the station of Abraham﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125] in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

Accordingly, the sentence in this respect is a fresh, independent beginning (*isti'nāf ibtidā'ī*).

The relative clause is a qualifier of the Name of Majesty. This clause was mentioned because of what it indicates of God's great power, and that people, who are among what is on the earth, are His servants. Therefore they must fear Him, not transgress His limits, and take account of themselves regarding the extent of their obedience to Him, for nothing hidden is concealed from Him. He is also capable of bringing good to them if they obey Him, and of punishing them if they disobey.

In it is also an honouring of the Qur'an, since it is among the affair that descends between the heaven and the earth.

The seven heavens have been discussed more than once. They are seven separate from one another, according to His words in Sūrat Nūḥ: ﴿Did you not see how God created seven heavens in layers?﴾ [Nūḥ: 15].

His words ﴿and of the earth the like of them﴾ are coordinated with ﴿seven heavens﴾, and this admits of two possibilities:

The first: that the coordinated element is His words ﴿of the earth﴾, the coordinated item being the word "earth", and the particle *min* (of) being redundant for emphasis, according to the view of the Kufans and al-Akhfash, who do not require that the redundant *min* occur in a context of negation, prohibition, interrogation or conditional. This is the more deserving of acceptance, even if it is not frequent in speech, and infrequency does not conflict with eloquence. The implied meaning is: "and He created the earth", and His words ﴿the like of them﴾ are then a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of ﴿the earth﴾.

The likeness of the earth to the heavens lies in the indication of the great power of God in their creation; that is, the creation of the earth is no less a sign of power than the creation of the heavens, since each of them has features indicating great power.

[p. 340]

This is the most apparent way to interpret the verse.

In the use of the singular word ﴿the earth﴾, rather than being put in the plural as the word "heavens" was, there is an indication that the two conditions differ.

The second possibility: that the coordinated element is ﴿the like of them﴾, and His words ﴿and of the earth﴾ are an explanation of "the like", so that what ﴿the like of them﴾ refers to is ﴿the earth﴾. In this case *min* is explanatory (*bayāniyya*), and there is in it the placing of the explanation before what is explained, which occurs and is not rare.

On this view, it is permissible that [the earth] be similar in sphericity, that is, like one of the heavens; that is, like one of the seven planets in that it travels around the sun like the planets. In that case what is in the verse would be among the scientific miracles which we mentioned in the tenth introduction.

Most of the exegetes made the likeness lie in the number seven, and they said: the earth is seven layers. Some of them said that they are seven flat layers separated by seas. This is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbās through the narration of al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ from him. Others said that they are seven strata, one above another, and this is the view of the majority. This approaches the view of the scholars of the earth's strata (geology), in establishing terrestrial strata, but these do not reach seven strata.

In al-Kashshāf it is said: "It is said that there is no verse in the Qur'an that indicates that the earths are seven except this one," end of quote. You have come to know that there is no indication in it of that.

Al-Māzarī said in his book *al-Mu'lim 'alā Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*, regarding the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Book of Pre-emption: "Whoever unjustly seizes a span of land, it will be hung around him from seven earths on the Day of Resurrection."

Our shaykh Abū Muḥammad 'Abd al-Ḥamīd wrote to me after I had parted from him, asking: "Has anything occurred in the Sharī'ah that indicates the earth is seven?" I wrote to him citing God's words ﴿God is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them﴾, and I mentioned to him this ḥadīth. He replied in his letter, mentioning that the verse is open to interpretation: whether "the like of them" means in shape and form, or in number. He also said that the report is one of the solitary reports (*akhbār al-āḥād*), and that the Qur'an, when it admits of more than one meaning, and a report that is not *mutawātir* (widely transmitted to certainty), cannot establish a definite judgment about it; and that the matter is not one of the practical rulings, so that one should not hold to apparent meanings and solitary reports in it. I replied to him again, arguing the remoteness of this interpretation from the Qur'an, and I expanded on that view, and I hesitated at the end of my book about the possibility of what he said. He then ended the correspondence, end of quote.

[p. 341]

You have now made clear that the singular "earth" indicates that it is one earth, and that the likeness in His words ﴿the like of them﴾ refers to likeness in the great creation. As for the ḥadīth, it concerns one of the matters of the Hereafter, and such matters differ from what is customary. Thus it is permissible that the usurper be encircled with the amount he seized, multiplied seven times in thickness and weight. Moreover, the number seven may be intended to express exaggeration in multiplication. Had the intended meaning been known layers, he would have said "from the seven earths", using the definite form. The words of 'Abd al-Ḥamīd are more inclined to verification than the words of al-Māzarī.

If we accept the majority's interpretation of His words ﴿and of the earth the like of them﴾ as likeness in the number seven, it is permissible to say that the seven are seven broad masses of the earth's surface separated by seas, which we call continents, though we do not mean by this designation the technical sense used in ancient or modern geography books. Rather they are natural continents, among which the inhabitants of some could not reach those of others in ages when there was no seafaring travel, and in later ages when sea voyage was still dreadful. These are: Asia together with Europe as one continent; Africa, a continent; Australia, a continent; North America, a continent; South America, a continent; Greenland in the north; and the Antarctic continent. Scattered parts of the earth in the seas are not taken into account. In this case *min* is partitive, because these conventional continents are parts of the earth.

All readers recited ﴿the like of them﴾ in the accusative. 'Āṣim, in a non-*mutawātir* reading, recited it in the nominative, as a subject (*mubtada'*).

The meaning of ﴿the command descends among them﴾ is: God's command, whether of creation or of obligation, is conveyed to those whom God commands to carry it, from among the angels, so that they may convey it; or to whomever God commands among the messengers to convey it on His behalf; or among people, so that they may know what it contains. All of this takes place between the heaven and the earth.

The *lām* in His words ﴿so that you may know﴾ is the *lām* of purpose (*lām kay*), and it is connected to "created".

The meaning: among what God intended by His creation of the heavens and the earth is that people should know God's power over all things and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all things. For the creation of those great creatures, their subjection, and the management of their order over the long course of time, indicate to the minds of reflective people that their Originator is capable of creating similar things; so they may infer from this that He is capable of all things. For their indication of the origination of what is lower than them is evident, and their indication of what is greater than them, though not witnessed, is by analogy of the absent to the present: the creator of their like is capable of what is greater. Furthermore, the management of those creatures with that same perfection witnessed in their order is evidence of the vastness of knowledge of their Originator and His comprehensiveness of the minute details of what is lower than them; and whoever has knowledge of that degree is not to be supposed to have knowledge other than encompassing all things.

Thus the knowledge meant by His words ﴿so that you may know﴾ applies to two kinds of knowledge: certain knowledge (*yaqīnī*) based on certain proofs composed of sensory and rational indication, and conjectural knowledge (*ẓannī*) based on conjectural proofs and indicators. Both kinds of knowledge lead to inference in rhetorical argument (*al-istidlāl al-khiṭābī*, with the *kh* vowelled with fatḥa).

Sūrat al-Taḥrīm

The sūrah which begins ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what God has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 1], and so on, is named "Sūrat al-Taḥrīm" in the books of Sunnah and the books of exegesis. In the narration of Abū Dharr al-Harawī of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, it is named by the phrase "Sūrat al-Lim Tuḥarrim", with the *lām* doubled. In al-Itqān it is called "Sūrat al-Lim Tuḥarrim", and in the Tafsīr of al-Kawāshī it is given as: with a hamzat waṣl, the *lām* doubled and kasra, the *mīm* with fatḥa, the *tā'* with ḍamma and unassimilated, and the *rā'* doubled with kasra followed by a *mīm*, by way of quoting the phrase ﴿why do you prohibit﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 1] and treating it as a name, with the definite article of specificity (*lām al-'ahd*) prefixed to that expression and the two *lām*s assimilated.

It is also called "Sūrat al-Nabī" (ﷺ). Al-Ālūsī said that Ibn al-Zubayr named it "Sūrat al-Nisā'". I say: I have not come across this, and the author of al-Itqān did not mention these two among its names.

The scholars of counting agree that the number of its verses is twelve.

It is Medinan. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: by the consensus of the scholars, and al-Qurṭubī followed him. Al-Itqān reports from Qatādah that its beginning up to the completion of ten verses is [Medinan], and what follows it is Meccan, as his statement is quoted. Perhaps he meant "up to ten verses", meaning that the tenth verse is Meccan, since it would be unlikely for the tenth verse to be Medinan and the eleventh Meccan.

In the chronological order of the revelation of the sūrahs of the Qur'an, it is counted as the hundred and fifth. It was revealed after Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt and before Sūrat al-Jumu'ah.

[p. 344]

His words ﴿God has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 2] indicate that it was revealed after Sūrat al-Mā'idah, as will come.

Its occasion of revelation was two incidents that occurred among the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The first: what is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ from 'Ā'ishah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) had drunk honey at the house of one of his wives. It is disputed whether that was Zaynab bint Jaḥsh, or Ḥafṣah, or Umm Salamah, or Sawdah bint Zam'ah; the more sound view is that it was Zaynab. 'Ā'ishah learned of this, so she and Ḥafṣah agreed that whichever of them he entered upon should say to him: "I smell maghāfīr on you; you have eaten maghāfīr." (Maghāfīr is the gum of the 'urfuṭ tree, and it has a fermented smell.) The Prophet (ﷺ) disliked that any smell should be found on him. They conspired in this only out of jealousy, that he would be detained at Zaynab's for a time in which he drank honey. He entered upon Ḥafṣah and she said that to him. He said: "Rather, I drank honey at so-and-so's, and I will never return to it." He intended by this to win Ḥafṣah's contentment in this matter, and he charged her not to tell 'Ā'ishah about it, because he disliked her anger. But Ḥafṣah told 'Ā'ishah, and then the verses were revealed.

This is the most sound of what has been narrated concerning the occasion of revelation of these verses. The prohibition is his statement: "and I will never return to it", for the Prophet (ﷺ) only says what is true. Sawdah used to say: "We have indeed forbidden it to him."

The second: what Ibn al-Qāsim narrated in al-Mudawwanah from Mālik, from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) made Umm Ibrāhīm, his slave-girl, forbidden, and he said: 'By God, I will not have intercourse with you.' Then he said: 'She is forbidden to me.'" Then God revealed ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what God has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives?﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 1].

[Page 345]

The detail of this report is what al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered with his umm walad (slave-concubine) Mariyah into the house of Hafsah, and Hafsah found him with her. Hafsah had gone out to her father's house. Hafsah said: 'You brought her into my house, and you did this with me among your wives only to demean me in your eyes.' He said to her: 'Do not mention this to 'A'ishah, for she is forbidden to me if I approach her.' It was said: Then Hafsah said to him: 'How can she be forbidden to you when she is your slave-girl?' So he swore to her that he would not approach her. Hafsah then mentioned it to 'A'ishah, and he took an oath of abstention (ila') that he would not enter upon his wives for a month." Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1]. This is a weak hadith.

* * *

The purposes of this surah include what its occasion of revelation contains: that no one should prohibit for himself what Allah has made lawful for him in order to please someone else, since that is not in his interest nor in the interest of the one whose pleasure he seeks. Therefore it should not be treated as a vow (nadhr), since there is no act of devotion (qurbah) in it, nor is it a divorce, because the one he prohibited was a slave-girl and not a wife. The welfare of each side lies only in what returns benefit to a person himself or benefits others in a way that is pleasing to Allah.

Also, it alerts the wives of the Prophet ﷺ that Allah's jealousy for His Prophet is greater than their jealousy for him, and more elevated in purpose.

And that Allah informs him of the events that concern him specifically.

And that whoever swears an oath and then sees that breaking it is better than keeping it, let him make expiation for it and do what is better. This has been expressly stated in the hadith of the delegation of 'Abd al-Qays, related by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and it was mentioned earlier in Surat Bara'ah (al-Tawbah).

And the instruction to wives that they should not excessively harass their husbands, for that may lead to weariness, then aversion, then separation.

And admonishing people by means of some family members educating others, and some of them advising others.

This is followed by a description of the punishment of the Hereafter and its bliss, and of the deeds of people, good and bad, that lead to either of them.

This is concluded with the setting forth of two examples of righteous women and their opposites, because of the honour it contains for the wives of the believers and their mothers.
